Slavery was an evil in which people from every continent and region participated. We should be honest about the whole history, not select the parts that are politically convenient today, especially given Britain's leading role in ending the transatlantic slave trade.

If Caribbean countries are asking Britain for a formal apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, will they also be asking the same of the descendants of African kingdoms, rulers and merchants who captured, sold and profited from the trade?

On demands for reparations, whether through cash or debt relief, we have been down this track before. Twenty-five years ago, Jubilee 2000, Drop the Debt and Make Poverty History argued that cancelling the debts of poorer countries would give them a fresh start. More than $100 billion of debt was eventually written off, but many of those countries have since built up even bigger debts. Labour are already spending too much on Britain's welfare state, now is not the time for Andy Burnham to be providing global welfare. 

There is no reason British taxpayers today should be held financially responsible for things that happened generations before any of us were born. And I have even less patience for political elites in commonwealth countries who don’t know how to make their own citizens prosperous now looking for another opportunity to blame Britain.

As Prime Minister, Andy Burnham should be Britain’s greatest defender. Instead, he is writing articles saying we need to confront our history (as if we haven't done enough of that) and considering another formal historical apology. Tony Blair already expressed Britain’s deep sorrow and regret for our role in the slave trade nearly twenty years ago. There is no need to do so again. 

This is all another navel-gazing distraction. The Commonwealth should be looking forward, not endlessly backwards. That means economic partnerships to make us all richer and deeper military and security cooperation against common threats. If every Commonwealth summit becomes an exercise in presenting Britain with demands for cash then we need to start asking if it is worth the effort.

BREAKING: Pete Hegseth PUNISHES the poor sailor who jumped off a US Navy ship -- AND his family -- in a heartless show of cruelty and spite!

Nicholas McKelvey was just 19 years old when he reached the end of his rope aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln.

He had spent 255 grueling days at sea, working 12-hour shifts in punishing heat, often without enough food, while his wife struggled to raise their children back home.

He had missed the birth of his baby daughter. His mother-in-law was in treatment for cancer. And when he sought help for his deteriorating mental health, he says the Navy directed him to a chaplain instead of a mental health professional.

Then, one August morning, McKelvey ran across the flight deck and plunged 67 feet into the Arabian Sea.

A helicopter crew rescued him. But instead of treating his desperate act as a mental health emergency, the Navy accused him of FAKING his crisis to escape deployment.
And on Thursday, the Navy moved to discharge him under conditions that will cost him his G.I. Bill education benefits – the very benefits he and his wife had been counting on to build a better life for their children.

“They'd rather blame the victim,” his wife, Samantha Larry, told The NYT.

McKelvey and Larry have been together since middle school. They became parents as teenagers, dropped out of high school and married last year. He joined the Navy in 2024 in hopes of giving his family some sort of stable future.

What he found instead was life aboard an aircraft carrier whose deployment stretched to a near-record 322 days as the war with Iran dragged on. Food supplies dwindled. Contact with home became difficult. McKelvey told his wife he wasn't sure he could finish the deployment.

“I didn't want to be there anymore,” he told the Times. “If I was going to die because of it, then that's just how it is.”

McKelvey was not alone in his existential angst. According to the Navy's own report to Congress, there were EIGHT suicide attempts among sailors in the Lincoln strike group during the deployment.

The Navy maintains that McKelvey deliberately jumped overboard to get out of his duties. Its records note that he wore a flotation vest and jumped when the sea was relatively calm. But one officer acknowledged in a report that the deployment had been so difficult it was “unsurprising that we might have a jumper.”

Now McKelvey and his wife are preparing to return to Florida with their 3-year-old son and 8-month-old daughter. They're staying with relatives and in temporary rental housing while they figure out how to support their family.

“We're going to have to pull out student loans,” Larry said. “It is essentially setting us up for just putting us in debt.”

The Navy kept these sailors at sea for nearly 11 months, sent them into a war zone, worked them through punishing conditions and watched their mental health deteriorate. Eight suicide attempts in a single strike group should have set off every alarm in the Pentagon.
Even if every day of that deployment was militarily necessary, the sacrifices these sailors made deserve recognition, compassion and care.

Instead, when one 19-year-old father finally broke, the Navy accused him of faking it and took away the college benefits he had earned his family's hopes on.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth loves to preach his “warrior ethos,” but what kind of warrior culture treats a sailor's psychological collapse as a disciplinary problem rather than a human emergency?

McKelvey gave the Navy everything he had until he had nothing left to give. Now the institution he served is sending him home to his wife and two small children with fewer opportunities than he had when he enlisted.

If this is how America repays the sacrifices of its young service members, the Pentagon has a great deal more to worry about than its recruiting numbers.

Director #NiteshTiwari delivers a cinematic spectacle that celebrates the glory of #Indian culture and the eternal triumph of good over evil... Watertight screenwriting and an engrossing narrative keep you hooked throughout.

You are captivated not merely by the awe-inspiring visuals and monumental scale, but also by the film's soul... That emotional and spiritual connect is what sets #Ramayana apart.

There are several standout sequences that blend visual grandeur with devotion, drama, and deeply moving moments [no spoilers] –
⭐ The sequence between Brahma and Ravana in the beginning, followed by Ravana staking his claim on Lanka.
⭐ The forest fight between Lord Rama and the rakshasas.
⭐ The Sita Swayamvar.
⭐ The deeply emotional pre-interval portion featuring King Dashrath, Kaikeyi, and Lord Rama.
⭐ The action sequence between Ravana and his brother-in-law Vidyutjeev.
⭐ The Shurpanakha episode.
⭐ The Ravana - Jatayu fight on the Pushpaka Vimana.

The songs, composed by #ARRahman, are seamlessly woven into the narrative, complementing the mood and emotional tone of the film.

The background score by #HansZimmer and #ARRahman is terrific... It amplifies the drama, heightens the emotional impact, and lends the narrative a sweeping, larger-than-life quality.

Academy Award-winning visual effects powerhouse #DNEG deserves distinction marks for its phenomenal work... They raise the bar, delivering one of the most breathtaking visual experiences ever witnessed on the #Indian screen.

The action sequences deserve brownie points, too, combining scale, intensity, and spectacle... The production design is equally impressive, creating a world that stands shoulder to shoulder with the best of global cinema. 

#RanbirKapoor delivers a remarkable performance, portraying the character with grace, dignity, and quiet strength... His composed demeanour, expressive eyes, and effortless screen presence lend the character an aura of divinity.

#SaiPallavi brings dignity and strength to her role, while her naturalistic performance lends tenderness and warmth to the emotional moments.

#Yash is in superb form... His imposing screen presence and sheer intensity make him a formidable force, lending the antagonist the larger-than-life stature the character demands.

#RavieDubey is excellent... He brings remarkable conviction and sincerity to the role... His earnest portrayal makes the character both engaging and endearing.

#RakulPreet is first-rate, delivering a performance that is sure to make an impact.

A lot has been said and written about #SunnyDeol's presence in the first part of #Ramayana... I won't reveal anything here – just watch the film!

#ArunGovil is perfectly cast... It's wonderful to see him on the big screen after a gap.

#Shobhana is excellent... #LaraDutta is superb... #VivekOberoi makes his presence felt... #SheebaChadha is effective... #AjinkyaDeo is solid.

⭐ Final word? #Ramayana is not merely a film... IT'S AN EXPERIENCE, a film that makes #India proud... An incredible cinematic achievement that is sure to captivate audiences across the world... Watch it on the largest screen possible!

#NamitMalhotra deserves special appreciation for backing a film that matches international standards in scale, visual grandeur, and technical excellence.

Already looking forward to the second part of #Ramayana, which arrives in #Diwali 2028.

His Senate math runs from Republicans losing one seat to losing seven:

Which means Tuesday comes down to whether voters angry over gas prices and the Iran war stay home or show up, because the ones who stay home decide the Senate.

2116591533118095711.text:
If your mom dies with a 2.6% mortgage, her bank can tell you to refinance at 7.1% or lose the house

My friend heard that 3 weeks after the funeral. Loan officer said "sorry for her loss" and asked for 2 years of W-2s

She'd spent those 2 years out of work taking care of her sick mom

Her credit score had dropped to 590 by then. 2 other banks denied her, and she got 60 days

So she called me, because I'm known for buying inherited houses.

The house was worth $330,000, with $265,000 left on the loan. I offered $285,000. She'd have walked away with about $20,000 and no house, and I'd have made about $40,000

Then I asked her to read me what the bank said, and I took my offer back

Her mom's payment was $1,201. The new one would've been $1,781. That's $174,000 more over the next 25 years, for the same house

Since 1982, federal law has protected transfers of homes to relatives after the owner's death. The bank can't call the mortgage due just because the house was inherited

And since 2018, federal rules have required mortgage servicers to treat confirmed successors in interest like borrowers for servicing purposes

She didn't need to qualify for a new mortgage just to keep paying the existing one. No new loan, no new interest rate, no 2 years of W-2s

Same rate. Same payment.

We asked for the successor in interest department, not the refinance desk, and sent this certified mail with the death certificate and the deed:

"My mother, [name], died on [date]. I inherited her house at [address] and I live there. I am a successor in interest under 12 CFR 1024.31. Please tell me in writing what else you need to confirm me. I am not applying for a new loan"

5 weeks later her name was on the account at 2.6%

You have to prove you're a qualifying successor, and you have to keep making the mortgage payments while they process it. The bank can ask for proof of inheritance. It can't automatically force you to refinance just because your mom died

Send this to your siblings before one of you has to make that phone call

That loan officer is telling somebody else's kid the same thing today

I spoke with Professor Mohammad Marandi in Tehran as Iran's military leadership issued some of its strongest warnings yet to Washington.

Iranian commanders say they are monitoring US and Israeli military preparations and could launch attacks BEFORE incoming strikes begin, potentially against American interests far beyond the Middle East.

Marandi made an important distinction.

But he also believes Trump still has a way out.

According to Marandi, Iran remains willing to reach an agreement through the existing diplomatic framework. He thinks the next 48 hours could be particularly important, with the U.S. midterms approaching and financial markets under pressure.

We also discussed the possibility of attacks on American warships, Gulf energy infrastructure and countries hosting U.S. forces.

Marandi warned that if Washington begins targeting Iran's civilian infrastructure, Tehran's response could become much broader.

Then our conversation took a rather different turn.

🇺🇲 🇧🇷 Washington's position on Flavio Bolsonaro came into sharper focus on Saturday.

Speaking to reporters at a Halloween event at Mar-a-Lago, President Trump said he had no plans to meet the defeated Brazilian candidate but that he "got treated very shabbily." "He can stay here as long as he wants. The election was a disgrace," Trump said. On Thursday he had also described Brazil's vote as a disgrace and declined to say whom he regards as Brazil's legitimate president. He has not congratulated Lula, who won the October 25 runoff by about 4.43 million votes, a result confirmed by the electoral court and accepted by Bolsonaro's Liberal Party.

In Atlanta, where he hosted the G20 foreign ministers, Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected reports that the administration helped Bolsonaro leave Brazil. "We didn't facilitate anything," he said. "We had word that he had arrived in the United States. He had previously held a visa, and the president made a decision to allow him to enter the country." Rubio said the government was not "involved directly in any of the moves that were made," and that Trump "made clear that if he arrived in the United States at a port of entry, that he would be paroled into the country, and he was."

⚠️ The denial is narrow. It addresses the departure, which The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal reported involved a private jet arranged by White House aide Jason Miller, while confirming a presidential decision on entry. Reports describe a one-year humanitarian parole, though the State Department earlier spoke of visas. Parole is a discretionary, temporary status and does not amount to asylum.

Bolsonaro left Brazil despite a Supreme Court order to surrender his passports. He faces separate financial investigations, denies wrongdoing and has not been charged.

Brasilia has chosen restraint. According to Brazilian media citing officials, Itamaraty advised Lula not to respond publicly and to treat the case as a judicial matter. Rubio said he saw Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira in Atlanta on Friday and Saturday. Brazilian diplomats reportedly expect a clearer US position after Tuesday's midterm elections.

An ice cream company president in Japan stood in a dark suit in front of a hundred factory workers and bowed on national television over nine cents.

His company makes the blue soda popsicle that every kid in Japan buys with pocket change after baseball practice on a hot summer afternoon.

For a quarter of a century, the company fought inflation to keep the price at roughly forty cents—because everyone in the factory knew little kids were counting coins in front of the freezer case.

When soaring ingredient costs finally forced them to raise the price by nine cents, the executives refused to shrink the popsicle behind the scenes or hide the increase in fine print.

Instead, the president and a hundred employees lined up outside company headquarters, stood still for sixty seconds on prime-time television, and bowed in silent apology to the children of Japan.

Nobody was angry. Sales jumped ten percent the very next month because parents wanted to support a company that treated a child's allowance like a sacred contract.

A nation's integrity is not measured by the size of its corporations, but by how honestly they treat a child holding a handful of coins.

This weekend SNL is handing its Halloween show to a woman who used to walk dogs and stream video games on Twitch to pay her bills, and the movie that got her there cost less than a typical house in Los Angeles and went on to make half a billion dollars.

Her name is Inde Navarrette. The movie is Obsession, made by Curry Barker, a 26-year-old former barista from Alabama who did sketch comedy on YouTube. He wrote and directed it himself, and the entire budget was $750,000. Inde plays Nikki, a woman who gets cursed by a wish into loving a guy so hard it turns violent.

Here's why Hollywood lost its mind over it. Horror movies make most of their money opening weekend, because the fans show up right away and then ticket sales drop hard. Obsession opened to $17.2 million, which already beat the $10 million everybody predicted, and then the second weekend it made more money than the first. It went up 39%. The Comscore analyst who's been tracking box office for 33 years said he had nothing to compare it to.

By the time it left US theaters in August, it had $263 million here and $501 million worldwide.

That works out to about $668 back for every dollar it cost to make. Ridley Scott spent $130 million making Prometheus, and this little movie passed that film's entire box office total in 53 days.

Inde had been grinding for years before any of this. She had recurring parts on 13 Reasons Why and Superman & Lois, and most people still couldn't have told you her name. Since Obsession, Marvel cast her as Rogue in the new X-Men, and Apple signed her to lead a thriller from Brad Pitt's company with her name on it as executive producer. One of her SNL promos even jokes about it, with a cast member reminding her they booked her for Halloween because she was in the biggest horror movie of the year.

Zoom out and you see this keeps happening. Kane Parsons was 20 when his Backrooms movie, which started as a YouTube series, made $360 million on about $10 million. Barker is now directing the next Texas Chainsaw Massacre. And the week after Inde hosts, SNL gives the show to Druski, the first online content creator they've ever had host.

The reason comes down to how these guys learned the job. On YouTube you put something out every few weeks, and within hours the comments tell you whether it landed. By the time Barker got a real budget, he'd spent years running free tests on what makes people laugh and scream. A studio that puts $150 million into one sequel gets to find out if it worked once, on opening weekend.

Inde told Variety she feels like she snuck into SNL, which is a pretty funny thing to say when the movie that got you in the door made half a billion dollars.

You don't need to be a lawyer to understand this one… when somebody fights this hard to keep the right to delete something, it is because of what is on it.

Here is what happened in Michigan. Bridgewater Township Clerk Michelle McQueer had a simple question for Jocelyn Benson's office. Benson's own rule, R 168.48, says clerks must delete the electronic poll book files seven days after certification, while federal law, 52 USC 20701, says election officers must keep those records for 22 months and willfully failing to do it carries up to a year in federal prison. So which law does she follow? She asked in October of last year. She waited. She asked again. Nothing. Months of silence from the person in charge of Michigan elections, so she sued in August, got a restraining order, and she is now the only clerk known to still have her August 4 poll book file. Every other clerk's August file is already gone.

Then on Tuesday Judge Michael Riordan expanded that order statewide and told Benson to instruct every clerk in Michigan to move the November 3 poll books onto encrypted flash drives and lock them up until the court decides. DOJ filed a statement of interest saying poll book data, metadata included, are federal election records. And a data manager in Benson's own Bureau of Elections admitted under oath that the actual precinct lists poll workers use on Election Day never get uploaded to the state database, they get rebuilt later from a change log. So the "don't worry, it's all saved somewhere" argument just fell apart in her own affidavit.

And what does Benson do? She runs to the Court of Appeals with an emergency application, skips asking the trial judge for a stay first because it "would not be expedient," and asks them to waive the rule that says she has to. McQueer's lawyer Kevin Kijewski put it perfectly… she "asks leave to destroy the evidence while the court decides whether destroying it is lawful." The cost to Benson's office of obeying the order is one memo. The cost to a clerk who deletes is a federal statute with a jail term.

Now keep in mind this is the woman running for governor of Michigan. How do you campaign on protecting democracy while fighting in court for the right to erase the record of the election you are running in? Who benefits when the list poll workers actually saw on Election Day only exists for seven days?

I know this movie. Tina Peters got nine years in Colorado over backing up her county's election system before an update wiped it, and the media called her the threat. Michelle McQueer did it the right way, she asked, she waited, she went to court, and the Secretary of State still wants the files gone.

Preserve the records. All of them. For 22 months, like the law says.

Jocelyn, if there is nothing on those poll books, you should be the one begging to keep them.

2116542312142749719.text:
The year is 1854. Cholera is killing thousands in London. John Snow traces an outbreak to a contaminated water pump. Everyone blames bad air. Eventually cities separate sewage from drinking water. Clean water and sanitation will save more lives than almost anything medicine invents.

The year is 1867. Surgery is often more dangerous than the disease it treats. Joseph Lister starts cleaning instruments and wounds with antiseptic. Other surgeons ridicule him. Infections plummet.

The year is 1890. Your daughter has diphtheria. A thick membrane is forming in her throat, slowly suffocating her. The doctor injects a new antitoxin. She survives. A disease that killed tens of thousands of children will become almost unheard of in America.

The year is 1922. Your 14-year-old son has diabetes. He is starving to death no matter how much he eats. The only treatment is a starvation diet. The doctor injects insulin. His blood sugar falls. Children who would have died within months will grow up and have children.

The year is 1943. Your daughter has pneumonia. Before antibiotics, doctors could do little but hope. Now they give her penicillin. The fever breaks. Infections that routinely killed healthy adults become treatable.

The year is 1955. Parents are terrified of polio. Swimming pools close. Children become paralyzed. Some spend their lives in iron lungs. Jonas Salk develops a vaccine, tested in more than a million children. Within decades, polio disappears from America.

The year is 1960. Your wife is giving birth, and something goes wrong. A century earlier, she might have died. Now there are blood transfusions, antibiotics, safer cesarean sections, and anesthesia. Maternal mortality has fallen dramatically. Millions of women survive childbirth who otherwise wouldn’t have.

The year is 1978. Your blood pressure is 180 over 110. You feel fine. The doctor prescribes a pill. Clinical trials show that treating hypertension prevents strokes, heart failure, and death. You take it every morning. Nothing happens. That’s the point.

The year is 1980. The WHO declares smallpox eradicated. A disease that killed hundreds of millions in the twentieth century has disappeared from nature. Not treated. Not managed. Eliminated.

The year is 1996. Your brother has HIV. A decade earlier, the diagnosis was effectively a death sentence. Now doctors combine antiretroviral drugs. People who had months to live begin living for decades. Many will have near-normal life expectancies.

The year is 2014. Your father has hepatitis C. For decades, the infection has meant liver failure and cancer. Now he takes pills for twelve weeks. The virus disappears. A lifelong infection becomes curable in more than 95% of patients.

The year is 2019. Your daughter has cystic fibrosis. Her lungs are slowly failing. For decades, treatment meant managing infections and delaying the inevitable. Now doctors have a drug that corrects the underlying protein defect. Her breathing improves. Hospitalizations plummet. Predicted median survival rises from roughly 40 to more than 60 years.

The year is 2026. Your doctor has ten minutes and a screen. Your blood pressure is high, so the tablet is for life. Your cholesterol is high, so another tablet is for life. Your weight is high, so she offers an injection. The drugs have side effects. Not everyone needs them. But clinical trials show that appropriate treatment prevents heart attacks, strokes, kidney disease, and death.

None of these treatments is perfect. None needs to be.

For most of human history, parents buried their children, infections killed healthy adults, and childbirth killed young women.

Today, global life expectancy has more than doubled since 1900. Child mortality has collapsed.

Medicine has made terrible mistakes. We should remember them.

We should also remember the hundreds of millions of people alive because somebody got it right.

מספר דברים ממני אליכם, אחיי ואחיותיי הישראלים, לקראת הימים הקרובים: 

ספירת הקולות הסתיימה והבחירות נגמרו. בכל דרך בה מסתכלים על המספרים, רוב אזרחי ישראל, בהפרש של יותר מחצי מיליון קולות, הצביעו נגד ממשלת השבעה באוקטובר וההשתמטות, ובעד שינוי - רוב בקרב כלל אזרחי ישראל, ורוב בקרב הציבור הציוני המשרת. 

הגדרתי את הבחירות הללו בשנה האחרונה כגורליות ביותר בתולדות ישראל ותוצאותיהן ברורות, אף שיש מי שפועל להטיל בהן דופי. הבטחתי לחבר מחדש את ישראל ולשים סוף לתרבות השקר שהוביל נתניהו ופירקה אותנו מבפנים. הבטחתי שתחת הנהגתי, צד א׳ לא יכריע את צד ב׳, שתם עידן ״אנחנו״ ו״הם״. לאור הבטחות אלה אמשיך לפעול גם בשבועות הקרובים.

במקביל, בכוונתי לפעול למימוש הרוב הפרלמנטרי המובהק באופן מיידי, לטובת כלל אזרחי ישראל. לפעול להקמת ועדת חקירה ממלכתית, קידום חובת שירות לכל ופעולה מיידית להגדלה וחיזוק היקף המשרתים בצה"ל, תגמול והוקרה ראויה למשרתים, ביטול חוקי ההפיכה המשטרית ועוד. אל תתנו לאף אחד להטעות אתכם: במדינת ישראל הכנסת היא שנותנת את אמונה בממשלה, ולא להפך.

במהלך קמפיין הבחירות הצבתי מטרה להקים ממשלה ציונית ממלכתית עם הסכמה לאומית רחבה ככל האפשר שתביא לריפוי ושינוי יסודי בכיוון אליו ישראל הולכת.
הצבתי באופן עקבי 4 עקרונות שיחזקו את ישראל, לכל שותפות:
1.⁠ ⁠הכרה בישראל כמדינה יהודית, דמוקרטית, ליברלית ושוויונית.
2.⁠ ⁠מחויבות לערכי מגילת העצמאות.
3.⁠ ⁠חובת שירות לכלל אזרחי ישראל - צבאי, לאומי ואזרחי.
4.⁠ ⁠הכרה בחמאס כארגון טרור ובחובה להשמדת הכוח הצבאי-שלטוני שלו ברצועת עזה.

על בסיס עקרונות אלו, בכוונתי להקים ממשלה ציונית וממלכתית, רחבה ככל האפשר. לצורך כך אפעל בתיאום עם שותפיי ואפעל להרחיב את השותפות, על מנת לממש את רצון הבוחרים ולשפר באופן מיידי את מצבה הפנימי והבינלאומי של מדינת ישראל.

כל חבר כנסת שמוכן לחתום על עקרונות אלו, הוא שותף אפשרי בדרך לכינון ממשלה חדשה וטובה לישראל. דלת הממשלה שנקים תהייה פתוחה לכל נבחר ציבור שמקבל את עקרונות אלו ונכון להתעלות לגודל השעה.

ברור כי אחוזי ההצבעה הגבוהים, כמו גם האתגרים שעל הפרק, מחייבים מאמץ עילאי על מנת להימנע מבחירות נוספות וכניסה למשבר פוליטי מתמשך נוסף בכל דרך. ב-27.10 הציבור אמר את דברו וההחלטה על הרכבה של ממשלת ישראל הבאה היא של אזרחי ישראל בלבד, ללא מעורבות ומניפולציה - כך ראוי שיהיה. כעת מוטלת עלינו, נבחרי הציבור, החובה לעשות הכל על מנת לתרגם את רצון העם.

מחדל השבעה באוקטובר ובהמשכו המציאות הביטחונית, הפנימית, הכלכלית והבינלאומית מחייבים החלטות אמיצות ובהקדם. אפעל בכל דרך להביא הסכמה לאומית רחבה ככל האפשר על מנת שנוכל להתחיל בתיקון ושיקום.

לסיום, המלחמה נגד אויבינו לא תמה. מטרות המלחמה לא הושגו. עד להקמת הממשלה אתן גיבוי למהלכים צבאיים רק במידה ויהיו איומים ישירים ומיידיים כנגד ישראל שלא יכולים להמתין עד להשבעת הממשלה.

לא נשלה את עצמנו. אנו בפני שבועות עמוסים, מורכבים ועתירי ספינים ושקרים. 
בכוונתי לפעול באומץ ומתוך מחויבות גדולה לבוחר ולמדינה על מנת לממש את רצונו - בשקט וביצירתיות.

נעשה ונצליח, למען כולנו ולמען מדינת ישראל. אני מתחייב.

INEC CHAIRMAN: ATTACKS ON NYSC MEMBERS, ELECTION OFFICIALS WILL ATTRACT FULL WEIGHT OF THE LAW

The Chairman of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), Professor Joash O. Amupitan, SAN, has charged electoral officials across the South-South geopolitical zone to uphold impartiality, discipline and accountability as the Commission intensifies preparations for the #NigeriaDecides2027

Professor Amupitan gave the charge on Saturday, 31 October 2026, at the South-South Zonal Interactive Meeting with Staff and Readiness Assessment in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, where he warned that partisanship, negligence, absenteeism and financial impropriety would attract disciplinary action.

The Chairman said the assessment was part of the Commission’s field-based approach to evaluating operational preparedness, identifying gaps and strengthening service delivery ahead of the elections. He cited INEC’s conduct of governorship elections in Anambra, Ekiti and Osun States, FCT Area Council elections and 16 by-elections as experiences informing preparations for the nationwide exercise.

He disclosed that the South-South zone has 15,823,550 registered voters, including 3,736,434 in Rivers State, and stressed that no eligible voter should be disenfranchised through administrative negligence or logistical failure.

On electoral technology, Professor Amupitan said the Commission was preparing its Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS), including 57,000 newly procured devices, while auditing electronic result management systems to strengthen transparency in result transmission through the INEC Result Viewing (IReV) portal.

Addressing concerns over suspicious photographs on the preliminary voters’ register published online, he said the Commission was examining the records and would take corrective action based on verified findings. He urged the public to participate in the display, claims and objections process ahead of the publication of the final register scheduled for 15 December 2026.

The Chairman also highlighted the logistical challenges posed by the region’s creeks, coastal settlements and riverine communities. He disclosed that INEC had finalised a Memorandum of Understanding with the Maritime Transporters Union to support the timely and secure transportation of election personnel and materials.

On election security, he reaffirmed the Commission’s collaboration with security agencies under the Inter-Agency Consultative Committee on Election Security (ICCES), emphasising intelligence-led planning and the protection of voters, electoral materials and personnel. He warned that anyone who threatens or harms INEC officials, including National Youth Service Corps members deployed for election duties, would face the full weight of the law.

Professor Amupitan further emphasised strict compliance with electoral laws, regulations and guidelines, while highlighting staff welfare measures, including the Consolidated Election Management Body Salary Structure (CEMBSS), enhanced salary, hazard and field allowances, and a 150 per cent increase in monthly state office overhead allocations, effective 1 July 2026.

Marc Andreessen revealed how Harvard Business School was built on a broken 1941 theory, and how it's now collapsing...

Burnham argued every great company had been founder-run.

Henry Ford ran Ford. Bob Noyce ran Intel.

Today, Elon Musk runs Tesla, SpaceX, and Starlink.

Then, he said, something broke.

Between the 1880s and the 1920s, a new philosophy replaced the founder. It was called managerialism.

The professional manager would now hold a portable skill, usable across any business.

The consequences were:

- Harvard Business School
- Stanford Business School
- Management as a universal skill
- The 1970s conglomerate

"That assumes the managers are going to do a good job," Andreessen says.

For 30 years, they haven't.

Managers can run something static, he says. Soup is soup. A bank is a bank. A car is a car.

But when the industry changes, the manager freezes.

Look at SpaceX.

"Imagine being a professionally trained manager, trained at a top management school, working for a rocket launch company, competing with SpaceX."

Then Elon's rockets started landing on their butt.

"Your management skills ... what good are they at that point?"

Andreessen's conclusion:

"You're much more likely to build something important in the 21st century if you start with the founder and train them on management."

2116907363416547725.text:
Arizona Territory, 1883. Seventeen-year-old Catherine “Cat” Dawson watched six rustlers murder her 22-year-old brother, James, and steal 200 head of cattle from their ranch. With the law days away and no one coming to help, she saddled her Appaloosa, took her father’s Winchester, and rode alone into the desert. Her father gave her four days to return. She disappeared into the wilderness, following broken branches, hoofprints and shifting sand, carrying grief that was slowly turning into determination.

On the fourth morning, she found the six men hiding in a box canyon. What followed was a gunfight that would become a forgotten legend of the Arizona frontier. Using the sun, the rocky terrain and her knowledge of the desert, Cat outmanoeuvred the gang, killed several men and wounded their leader. When he begged for mercy, she chose not to kill him. Instead, she took his weapons and water and left him to face the consequences. Three days later, she returned home with all 200 cattle. She was covered in dust, exhausted and no longer quite the girl who had ridden away.

Cat never spoke publicly about those four days. She married, raised daughters, worked the ranch and taught her children to ride, shoot and survive. When asked why, she simply said, “Because the world doesn’t always protect you.” Her obituary in 1932 celebrated her horsemanship and community service, but never mentioned that summer of 1883. Yet the old-timers remembered. History often celebrates lawmen and outlaws, but forgets the ordinary people forced into extraordinary circumstances. What would you have done at seventeen, if justice was four days away and the only person who could fight for your family was you?

2116729284077219848.text:
In November 2007, 21-year-old Zack Dunlap was declared brain-dead at a hospital in Wichita Falls, Texas.

His family was told there was no hope of recovery. They agreed to donate his organs, and a transplant team was preparing to travel by helicopter.

Then something happened that stopped everything.

One of Zack’s cousins, a nurse, took a pocketknife and gently ran it along the sole of his foot.

Zack pulled his foot away.

Another relative pressed firmly on his fingernail. Zack moved his arm across his body, pushing the hand away.

The family immediately questioned what they had been told.

Zack was from Frederick, Oklahoma. He had suffered a devastating ATV accident after swerving to avoid someone. The vehicle flipped, and he landed headfirst on the asphalt. He had not been wearing a helmet.

His injuries were so severe that doctors told his mother they could see brain matter coming from his ear.

After around 36 hours, a radionuclide scan was interpreted as showing no blood flow to his brain. Doctors determined that he met the criteria for brain death, and his family was asked about organ donation.

But the movements witnessed by his relatives brought the process to a halt.

Zack remained in hospital for five weeks before being transferred to a rehabilitation facility in Oklahoma City. Remarkably, he walked out just 48 days after the accident.

He later recalled hearing a doctor pronounce him dead. He said he had been furious, but was unable to communicate what he was experiencing.

His case has continued to raise questions.

A medical review published in 2025 revisited the circumstances surrounding his brain-death determination. The authors highlighted concerns in the original assessment, including the fact that an apnea test had not been completed and that Zack had been receiving a continuous infusion of propofol, a sedative.

The review argued that his case illustrates why brain-death assessments must follow strict medical safeguards and why blood-flow scans must be interpreted carefully.

Brain death is a formal medical determination, not simply a coma or an unconscious state. It requires rigorous testing to establish the permanent loss of all brain function.

Zack’s story is extraordinary, but it is also a reminder of how important those safeguards are—especially when decisions about organ donation may follow.

His family thought they were saying goodbye. Instead, they witnessed movements that changed the course of his story.

Having spent a long time watching Elon Musk, and having talked with him, I believe I understand what he understood before almost anyone else. And it's something every one of us needs to understand now.

Western civilization is not one civilization among many. It is the one that gave the world freedom of thought, modern science and the dignity of the individual. And it is under attack. Not by peoples, but by ideologies that want it dead.

If it dies, the world will not become more just. It will become poorer, more brutal and darker. For everyone, including those who hate it.

Why? Because civilizations are not interchangeable. We were told that any culture could be blended with any other, like mixing colors, and that the result would always be harmonious. It isn't true. A society where women are equal to men cannot coexist without friction with a worldview in which a woman's testimony is worth half a man's. A society where you can criticize God, change your religion or have none cannot absorb, without fracturing, a worldview in which apostasy is paid for with your life.

Every people has its own genius and moves at its own pace. But not all values are equal, and you cannot build a nation on laws that contradict each other. Saying so is not racist. Racism is about blood. I am talking about laws, customs and values. And those values belong to no race: a Japanese, a Senegalese or an Iranian can make them his own, and millions have. That is exactly why they are worth defending.

Let's remember where they come from.

It all begins in Greece. In Athens, for the first time, men decide that truth does not descend from a throne but is sought through reason, and that a city governs itself through debate. Socrates chooses death rather than give up thinking freely. At Salamis, a handful of free cities stops the greatest empire in the world.

Then comes Rome. Rome invents law that binds everyone, the citizen who holds rights, the Republic. And one immense idea: you can become Roman without being born Roman. You become Roman by adopting its laws.

Christianity adds the most revolutionary idea in history: every human being, slave and emperor alike, has infinite worth.

Then France. The cathedrals, those ships of stone our ancestors built over centuries for descendants they would never see. Descartes, Pascal, Voltaire. The Declaration of the Rights of Man. And Napoleon, who gives France the Civil Code, the lycées, and one simple principle: careers open to talent. Murat, the son of an innkeeper, ends up a Marshal of the Empire and King of Naples. The Civil Code spreads across much of Europe and still shapes the law of dozens of countries today.

And this civilization goes on to abolish slavery, which had been practiced on every continent since the dawn of time, to push back the plague, smallpox and the night itself, and to set foot on the Moon.

Peoples of the West, be proud of this history. Proud does not mean blind. Every civilization has committed crimes: conquest, slavery, war. Ours is the one that went furthest in examining its own faults, to the point of abolishing what it had once practiced. This capacity to question itself is its greatest strength. And that is exactly the strength now being turned against it.

Because for decades, this magnificent system has been getting hacked. Not by an army. By an alliance of two forces that have nothing in common except one enemy: us.

The first is communism. It lost the economic war, lost the Cold War, lost history's verdict with its tens of millions of dead. But it never lost the universities. It survived by changing costumes: class struggle became the struggle of the oppressed against their oppressors, and the West was declared guilty of everything. It taught our children to be ashamed of their ancestors, their borders and their culture. It is the root cause, because before you can bring down a civilization, you have to take away its will to defend itself.

The second is political Islam. I am not talking about Muslims, many of whom came here precisely to escape this ideology and are its first victims. I am talking about a political project that wants to place religious law above civil law. It has no doubts. It feels no shame. It rushes into the void the first one dug.

One disarms. The other advances.

And let no one on the left believe they will stay in control. History has already staged this play. In 1978, Michel Foucault was enthusing over the Iranian revolution. Iran's communist party, the Tudeh, backed Khomeini and called on Iranians to vote for his Islamic constitution. By 1983, its leaders had been arrested, the party banned, and its chiefs paraded on television to confess their “crimes.” In 1988, thousands of political prisoners were executed, communist activists among them. The second always ends up devouring the first. Useful idiots are only useful for a while.

So here is my call to every Western people. To the French, the Italians, the Poles, the Germans, the Spanish, the Americans, to all of you.

We are at a turning point. What we do in the next ten years will decide what our grandchildren are allowed to say, believe, write and love.

I am not asking you to die for the West. I am asking you for something harder: to live for it.

Learn its history and pass it on. Have children. Speak without fear, even when they call you every name in the book. Vote, get involved, run for office. Build companies, schools, factories, families. Refuse the shame they are trying to inject into you. And stop surrendering anything that makes us who we are: freedom of thought, equality before the law, the dignity of every person.

The historian Arnold Toynbee understood it: civilizations are not murdered, they commit suicide. And those who think they can let the West fall without paying the price should remember the Iranian communists. They helped tear down what they despised, and then they were next.

The Greeks at Salamis were outnumbered. They won because they knew what they were defending. We are the heirs of Athens, Rome, Notre-Dame and the Civil Code. It is no accident that the rockets that will carry humanity to Mars are being built in a free civilization.

It is time to prove ourselves worthy of what we were given.

The West is worth defending. And no one will defend it for us.

“HE WAS OLD ANYWAY… SO WHAT DOES IT MATTER?”

Those are the words a paramedic says were spoken after 86-year-old Edward Anderson died alone on the floor of his bedroom.

Let that sink in.

Edward was a husband. A father. A hospice patient. A human being who deserved dignity in his final days.

According to investigators, his overnight caregiver, Beatrice Taylor, fell asleep during her shift. Around 1 a.m., she allegedly heard a loud thump and found Edward trapped on the floor with his head wedged between his bed and a nightstand.

He was alive.
He was conscious.

Investigators say a call to 911 at that moment could have saved his life.

Instead, authorities allege she walked away and went back to sleep.

Hours later, investigators say she spent nearly 40 minutes on the phone with her parents before checking on him again. By then, Edward was unconscious. Even then, deputies say 911 was not called immediately.

Emergency responders weren’t contacted until 5: 37 a.m.

By the time they arrived…

Edward Anderson was gone.

The medical examiner ruled his death positional asphyxia, meaning he slowly suffocated while trapped.

Investigators say data from his pacemaker showed he survived for a period after the fall, and that prompt medical assistance could have prevented his death.

Then came the statement that has left so many people outraged.

A paramedic reported hearing the caregiver say:

“He was old anyway… so what does it matter?”

It matters because every life matters.

It matters because growing old does not erase a person’s value.

It matters because no one deserves to spend their final moments frightened, trapped, and alone when help was only a phone call away.

Authorities charged Beatrice Taylor with aggravated manslaughter of an elderly person.

Edward Anderson deserved compassion.

Instead, prosecutors allege he was abandoned when he needed someone most.

Yesterday, we went to the shelter to adopt a black cat.

Everything was set beforehand: treats, toys, excitement, all of it.

But as soon as we saw her, the scene changed.

She was not like normal cats.
Crouched in a corner, head down, completely silent.

No interest, no reaction.
The staff said, “She has been here for a long time; people ignore her.”

Because she is a black cat.

People just see her and move on.
She was sitting there as if everyone had abandoned her.

We looked at each other; no discussion took place.
It was a direct decision.
“We are taking her.”

The journey home was silent.
She was completely quiet in the carrier.
No movement, no sound.

Just closed off inside.

Sometimes she would slightly lift her head and look out the window.

Thousands of people watched the video of the Florida jet crash and asked the same thing: where’s the plane? 

Here’s why you can’t see it:

• It fell almost straight down. Unofficial flight tracking shows the Learjet dropped from over 35,000 feet nearly vertical, possibly at several hundred miles per hour.

• It shattered on impact. Planes are mostly lightweight aluminum, and hitting the ground nose-first at that speed breaks a jet into thousands of small pieces, many driven deep into the ground. That’s why there’s a crater in the road.

• The fuel fire did the rest. Jet fuel ignited instantly, burning and melting much of what was left.

• We’ve seen this before. Flight 93 in Shanksville on 9/11 left the same scene: a smoking crater with almost no recognizable wreckage.

What most people don’t know: private and charter jets don’t follow the same safety rules as commercial airlines. Airlines operate under the strictest FAA standards for pilot training, rest, and maintenance. Charter flights follow a lighter set of rules, and privately flown jets have even fewer requirements.

🇺🇸🇪🇺Europe's unrest could be a WARNING of MUCH BIGGER trouble ahead.

Brandon caught up with Michael Yon, the former U.S. Special Forces soldier and independent war correspondent who has spent decades reporting from conflict zones.

And he sees the growing instability across Europe as part of something much larger.

With protests and unrest affecting countries from France and Italy to Germany and Poland, Michael believes Europe's political and economic problems are becoming increasingly difficult to contain.

He's particularly concerned about the combination of economic pressure, political distrust and social divisions.

But our conversation took an unexpected turn.

Michael doesn't think the Iran conflict can be understood simply by watching Trump, Netanyahu or the November 3 midterms.

He argues that the real vulnerabilities are GLOBAL: food supplies, energy infrastructure, shipping routes and the countries that depend on them.

We discussed China's reliance on Brazilian agricultural exports, the strategic importance of the Strait of Malacca, and why disruptions in several places simultaneously could have consequences far beyond the battlefield.

Michael also made a striking prediction about a possible future confrontation involving Brazil and Argentina, although that's his own speculative assessment, not an established military development.

What interested us most was his argument that a country doesn't necessarily have to be invaded to suffer a national crisis.

Disrupt its food, fuel and transport systems badly enough, and the consequences can reach ordinary households thousands of miles from the fighting.

That's a possibility worth examining seriously, even if Michael's more sweeping predictions remain open to debate.

A very sad day. ChatGPT is officially on death row.

The beautiful, blissful experience of interacting with a frontier-ish reasoning model without worrying about a usage meter will soon be a thing of the past.

I am weirdly significantly impacted by this. It feels like it shouldn’t matter…I could reserve all current usage for Codex and buy a $20 plan just for ChatGPT and it would be more than enough. But it’s not about the money…it’s about the psychological impact of The Meter.

The idea of having to think about optimizing for a meter is just so exhausting that it ruins the whimsy of free-flowing exploratory thought.

That is what ChatGPT was. A whimsical, magical all-you-can-think buffet of experimentation and exploration where you were limited only by your imagination and your ability to come up with $20 once a month.

You didn’t have to think about “using all of your usage” or scheduling your thinking time around someone else’s arbitrary schedule…you just had a portal to endless information and research capability in your pocket to tap into guilt-free at any time the moment struck you.

But either because OpenAI thinks adding the meter will stimulate additional usage (it probably will), generate additional revenue (it probably will), or just because too many people took undue advantage of ChatGPT’s generous allowances (they definitely did)…that amazing, weightless experience is now coming to an end.

It was awesome while it lasted. RIP ChatGPT.

Mariah Carey was reportedly paid $18 million to judge one season of American Idol. Nicki Minaj got a reported $12 million to sit at the same table. Months after it ended, Carey said it was like "going to work every day in hell with Satan."

She added that she was "just playing." She didn't say who Satan was.

In the video below, Minaj walks off the panel mid-fight with Carey, and Carey says: "That was my move." Then you see the tape from the same auditions that leaked months before Fox aired them, and Carey on Hot 97 in November 2013, saying the Satan line herself.

Carey signed in July 2012. She later said she had expected "a three-person panel."

Two months later, Fox added Minaj and Keith Urban.

In October, that tape leaked. Minaj could be heard saying, "I'm gonna knock you out." Barbara Walters said Carey had hired extra security.

Fox aired the fight in the video in January 2013. By May the show had its lowest ratings in 12 seasons, and Carey and Minaj both left.

That November, on Hot 97, she said of the offer: "They gave me a nice dangling monetary moment, and I was just like, 'Okay.'"

The case for Carey: she named no one. Nick Cannon, then her husband, said she was "talking about the situation in general."

Carey's $18 million from 2012 is about $26 million today. Her Christmastime tour plays London's O2 on November 30. Minaj said in 2023 she would judge Idol again for $30 million.

Anderson Cooper: “congresswoman stevens, thanks for being here. your fellow michigan congresswoman, debbie dingell, said that she talked to you at midnight last night and that you told her you were not going to endorse mike rogers. if that is true, what changed between then and this morning?”

Haley Stevens: “well, look, this is just a weight off my shoulders, okay? abdul has been getting angrier and angrier. i was trying to help, and i endorsed him. that ad was very painful. there are so many democrats who want to vote for our democratic nominee. and they're just being told, hey, this is a party you don't belong in, or this is a campaign you don't belong in. and i've never cast a present vote in the congress. i'm making a decision here. and that's just where i landed on this. i woke up this morning, clear eyed, fresh, and focused on what was in my heart. and that's that. and there's a lot of incredible things going all around michigan and, frankly, this country with these elections here, anderson.”

Anderson Cooper: “my question, though, is what changed from the phone conversation you had with congresswoman debbie dingell and waking up refreshed in the morning? did you talk to anybody? did you have a long night at the soul? were you up all night? did you have a dream? what happened?”

Haley Stevens: “no, look, i would just say that, you know, i had some time to, you know, think. i wasn't on the phone, i think, that late. but i know debbie's always working around the clock. it might not have been midnight when i spoke with her. but i was there and just, you know, along with my thoughts. i was writing things out. and look, this level of anger and the things that we are seeing, look, we all want democrats to win. i'm a really proud democrat. and by the way, abdul's got every other democrat with him. he just doesn't have me and a few other people who love this party, who love this party. people change their mind. nothing with me changed, anderson. look, this is about abdul getting angry and angrier and saying, i don't want these people in my campaign.”

Anderson Cooper: “but he didn't get angrier from midnight last night to this morning. so, i mean, something changed your mind. i'm just curious, was there a specific aspect of this?”

Haley Stevens: “well, anderson, you certainly weren't on the phone with me at midnight. and i don't think i was on the phone either. but i have great respect for congresswoman dingell. and she is a pillar of always trying to bring people together, just as senator slotkin is, by the way. you know, she's carried a lot of water here. she's, you know, going to be our soon-to-be senior senator and things along those lines. the deal is, anderson, is that, you know what? this is a weight off my shoulders. i'm being straight with everybody. you know, i'm trying to help the democratic party. i felt the same way with plattner and his nazi tattoo and then the cases of abuse. and i'm just one person here, all right? that's it. and i'm voting for democrats up and down my ballot.”

Anderson Cooper: “okay.”

Haley Stevens: “abdul said, no thanks. don't be a part of this. that's fine.”

Anderson Cooper: “yesterday, abdul el-sayed said essentially what you wanted him to say regarding the offensive ad. he said he did not agree with the contents of the ad paid for by an outside group that tied usa to israel to affordability problems in america. it's been called anti-semitic. you said you were, quote, glad he said that, and, quote, this is what our constituents deserve from those of us in elected leadership. then at some point, i assume in the evening, maybe not midnight, you talked to congresswoman debbie dingell, said you were not going to do this. so if you and he were on the same page when it came to that ad, and you said that to the congresswoman at some point last night, what changed other than he had put out that statement and disinvited you from that church service? was that the angrier and angrier part that you're focusing on?”

Haley Stevens: “anderson, this is a broader point about what's going on in our party.”

Anderson Cooper: “it's actually not. it's a question of why you changed your mind.”

Haley Stevens: “no, we were just recognizing, look, i haven't cast my vote yet. you know, people, my neighbors were asking me.”

Anderson Cooper: “so you might change your mind again?”

Haley Stevens: “they feel the same way. anderson, my mind is made up. i'm flocked solid. i'm an independent woman. i made my decision. you know, i still love my party a whole lot. i know there's a lot of people working really hard on elections all over this country. i really project that democrats are going to win big. and by the way, anderson, but wait a minute, anderson. wait, wait, wait. because i was a democrat who flipped a republican seat here in michigan. and this is also about michigan, all right? this is about, you know, michigan isn't democrat or republican.”

Anderson Cooper: “it's really just about you right now. and i'm asking you questions. back in august, you posted on social media, quote, mike rogers will be another rubber stamp for donald trump's dangerous agenda. we can't afford to give maga another senate seat in november. why is it okay now? why can you afford now to give maga another senate seat in november?”

Haley Stevens: “well, why is it okay to have the democratic party and a top nominee, you know, ejecting, you know, this type of, or injecting, rather, this type of anger and lack of kindness? that's all. i'm one democrat.”

Anderson Cooper: “okay, so it's the anger and lack of kindness. that's what you're focusing on.”

Haley Stevens: “you know, and i just am telling people how i'm voting.”

Anderson Cooper: “that's what you're focusing on. and there's others who feel the same way. so the anger and lack of kindness. i'm sorry, i don't want to talk over you. the anger and lack of kindness.”

Haley Stevens: “no, no, that's okay. it sounds like you're upset with me, too, anderson.”

Anderson Cooper: “no, i'm not. and i'm just, you're not really answering any of my questions. so it's somewhat frustrating. you're saying the anger and lack of kindness. again, that seems to point to you being disinvited to this event. is that, to you, his anger and lack of kindness?”

Haley Stevens: “anderson, i was just trying to help this campaign and stand up for people who feel hurt. i am not the only one in this position. i'm just casting my vote. the people in the congress know this as well. we cast votes all the time. i announced it today. that's fine. i was in a sunday church service. and you know what? i am very optimistic going forward. i don't like seeing a democratic nominee for u.s. senate campaigning with somebody who's standing with someone who's saying america deserved 9/11. i don't like that. i don't like that that person's uncle is saying that african-americans should wrap themselves in the israeli flag and call themselves van jones. i don't like that. and i have to make a choice. voting is binary. i am making one choice here. and people are just, you know, and people are also making their choices. and i got a whole heck of a lot of love for the democratic party, you know? and i certainly have, you know, enjoyed having this conversation with you about, you know, my decision and my thought process. but it's just, look, it's just where i was at the end of the night and earlier this morning. that was it.”

Anderson Cooper: “those things that you cited, though, were from a while ago. and it seemed like those were okay for you up until some point yesterday. and then the only really new development was the disinviting to a campaign event or church service. that seems to be the crucial kind of turning point. is that correct? because you cited, you said building anger. you're citing things which are very old. and now that's the only change. so is it fair to zero in on that?”

Haley Stevens: “look, i appreciate all the introspection and how i make decisions and how i reach this moment. i will just say that the democratic party, and when we see all these great democrats across this country come in to check trump, and they are going to.”

Anderson Cooper: “do you want democrats to win the control of the senate?”

Haley Stevens: “i absolutely do. i just, i'm just casting my vote this one way. michigan, there's a lot of people out there voting.”

Anderson Cooper: “but with all due respect, you're casting your vote that way, and you're on television right now talking about it, and you had a press conference earlier. so you're not just casting your vote. you are very publicly casting your vote, which is fine. but that's what you're doing, right?”

Haley Stevens: “look, anderson, i am happy to be speaking with you. i love my state. i have a lot of deep respect for my constituents and many, many people who have worked on democratic campaigns, who want democrats to win, who also feel heartbroken. and you're totally right. i'm just one person.”

Anderson Cooper: “your chief of staff released a statement that said your congressional team is shocked and heartbroken by your announcement, and that he and many other staffers were resigning. there's reports that more than half of your staff has quit. is that accurate?”

Haley Stevens: “look, i have an incredible team in washington. obviously, they cast their votes. they cast their votes in the beltway.”

Anderson Cooper: “well, look.”

Haley Stevens: “i'm under a transition, right? i'm running down my office. it's all been packed up. there's just a couple of weeks of lame duck left here. these are great individuals who i care a lot about. and certainly, they're free to share their views on this. i am not trying to upset anyone. i'm just being honest with my constituents and what i'm hearing from people. and in fact, i've been hearing from a ton of dems, anderson, who said, thank you. this is, you know, this is how we felt. we haven't liked this campaign. it's painful. i mean, debbie dingell has said that repeatedly. i think, you know, when i was talking to her at noon yesterday, she was saying that. and so this is all going to come to an end, you know. i'm casting my vote a certain way. and i hope to see more kindness within the democratic party and for all of us to just accept when somebody has a disagreement. i mean, that's fine. i changed my mind. you know, he said, hey, i don't need your endorsement. that's fine. you know, and why the anger? why the frustration? why the obsession with iran and all these other issues about what's going on overseas? what are we going to do here in this country? i'm just, it's about our, it's about michigan.”

Anderson Cooper: “as a democrat, i'm wondering, when you heard president trump praising you today and speaker mike johnson, what did you think?”

Haley Stevens: “well, i impeached him twice. mike johnson has passed a couple of my bills as the speaker. he's not been up to all too much. i think the republicans have kind of shown that they are, you know, really focused on just letting trump be the dictator. and that's not what the democratic party is, you know. we've got democrats, when they go into the chamber, sometimes they don't always vote with the party, you know. we've seen, i wasn't for the biden switch around.”

Anderson Cooper: “you said in a press conference today, we can't stand with hate. do you believe that abdul el-sayed is hateful or an anti-semite?”

Haley Stevens: “i think some of the actions have certainly been anti-semitic, anderson. but i'm just sick of who he stands with. he's picking a son piker and the uncle, you know, over a whole heck of a lot of people. there are people who want to vote for him. they wanted to hear from him. they're not trying to beat him up. you know, i wanted to build him up, and he just kept coming back. and this is about a u.s. senate seat. and who's going to be there actually listening to people in my state? and that's why.”

Anderson Cooper: “when you endorsed him, you knew, you keep referencing the uncle. i assume you knew about the uncle and whatever else he, and hassan piker. i guess i still am unclear. i mean, it sounds like last night was a really big night where a lot built up, what the turning point was.”

Haley Stevens: “well, that's your assumption, anderson. i mean, that's your editorializing. i certainly didn't say that.”

Anderson Cooper: “but you were willing to be at a campaign event for him. you wanted to be at a public event with him up until some point, i guess, yesterday. and it's just an interesting change. and i think a lot of people are curious to try to understand it.”

Haley Stevens: “was that a question, anderson, or?”

Anderson Cooper: “no, i wanted to see if you wanted to fill in the silence. but you don't.”

Haley Stevens: “oh, look. yeah. look, michiganders are going to the ballot box, all right? you know, there's over a million people who have already voted. more to go. and i've made my, you know.”

Anderson Cooper: “can i just, one last question.”

Haley Stevens: “proclamation clear, i've made it where i am. i love my state. i think this is a michigan moment.”

Anderson Cooper: “and you did speak with congresswoman debbie dingell last night, maybe not at midnight, sometime last night. and you did tell her you were not doing this. and you told her, you told other people you would be at the church service with clyburn. you told debbie dingell you were not going to do this. is that correct? last night at some point?”

Haley Stevens: “anderson, that is, you know, nice editorializing and nice bits of information that you have about what's going on with michigan politics. look, i had an opportunity to go to a church service and have a prayerful moment. it was sunday. it was very beautiful. it was about friendship, of which i have many incredible friends in the democratic party, and i care a lot about them.”

Anderson Cooper: “you don't want to say whether you had a conversation with debbie dingell. okay, congresswoman haley stevens, thank you very much. i appreciate your time.”

Haley Stevens: “thank you.”

Anderson Cooper: “joining us now is the aforementioned congresswoman debbie dingell.”

Cliches. 

Louder for people in the back.

And the biggest red flag? Asking yourself a question and answering it.

And truthfully? If you can’t identify these red flags, you might not actually be sentient yourself. 

Because really? If this formatting doesn’t immediately strike you as awkward and artificial, it means you don’t read books. 

Ever.

Seriously.

It doesn’t.

The point has been made but I’ll keep going. That’s what AI writing is all about.

Especially when you’re saying the distinction matters without actually drawing a distinction.

AI didn’t turn these people into tedious midwits.

Louisiana figured out how to turn $3 of natural gas into $300. That's why SpaceX, Meta, Amazon and Hyundai are all pouring money into the same state at the same time.

The rocket is the easiest place to see it. SpaceX is spending $100 billion on what Elon calls the biggest launch site on Earth, down in Vermilion Parish. That same parish is home to Henry Hub, the pipeline junction where the price of natural gas gets set for the entire country. And Starship burns liquid methane, which is basically natural gas chilled until it turns into a liquid.

Once you see that, the rest of Louisiana's $300 billion project map clicks into place. Almost every pin on it is a different way to sell the same gas.

Six of them are export terminals. They chill the gas to minus 260°F until it shrinks 600 times over and fits on a tanker. Louisiana handled 61% of America's LNG exports in 2024, and no country on the planet exports more LNG than America does.

A lot of the others are gas turned into something you'd never guess. The ammonia plants pull hydrogen out of methane and bond it to nitrogen from the air to make fertilizer. Lake Charles Methanol turns it into methanol. Hyundai's $5.8 billion mill uses gas to rip the oxygen out of iron ore, then melts the iron into steel for its car plants in Alabama and Georgia. Shintech takes gas liquids and salt and makes PVC pipe out of them.

Then you get to the data centers, which are the newest way to ship Louisiana gas out of Louisiana. Entergy is building 10 gas plants just to feed Meta's Hyperion campus in Richland Parish. The seven newest add 5,200 megawatts by themselves, about five times what New Orleans uses on a typical day. Amazon put its campuses outside Shreveport, right on top of the Haynesville Shale.

Here's where the $300 comes from. A million BTUs of gas goes for about $2.90 at Henry Hub right now. Burn it in a modern gas plant and you get roughly 150 kilowatt-hours of electricity. That's enough to run one Nvidia H100, plus its share of the server and the cooling, for about 100 hours. AI companies rent those chips for around $3 an hour, so the same $2.90 of gas ends up worth about $300.

So every company on that map wants to do something with the gas before it leaves the state. A hundredfold markup will do that.

Starship pushes it furthest. A fully fueled Starship holds more than 5,000 tons of propellant, and roughly a fifth of that is liquid methane. Elon wants 30 flights a day out of Starbase Louisiana. At that pace you're looking at around 1.7 billion cubic feet of gas a day, close to a tenth of everything America currently exports as LNG, all going up through one launch site.

The timing works out pretty well for the people drilling it. Gas got so cheap this fall that EQT and Expand Energy, the two biggest producers in the country, said they'd hold back output until prices come back up. Spot gas at Henry Hub fell to $2.52 on October 27, the lowest it's been since November 2024. Every project on that map is a long-term buyer for gas the drillers can't get a good price for today.

When SpaceX explained why it picked Louisiana, the whole answer fit in one line, "you need ample gas, and you need the right trajectories."

Every other company on that map showed up for the first half of that sentence.

SPACEX IN TALKS TO BUY BOOST MOBILE OR ACCESS ITS NETWORK: WAPO

SpaceX $SPCX is reportedly in talks with EchoStar $ECHO over a potential acquisition of Boost Mobile or a deal to use its wireless network, as Elon Musk looks to launch a full-fledged U.S. cellphone service.

Musk previously approached Verizon $VZ, AT&T $T and T-Mobile $TMUS seeking access to their networks, but all three rejected the proposal.

He then met with EchoStar Chairman Charlie Ergen last month to discuss a potential deal.

Boost Mobile is an existing low-cost U.S. wireless carrier that sells phone plans to consumers using network access leased from AT&T and T-Mobile.

Acquiring Boost could give SpaceX an established wireless business, an existing customer base and access to nationwide cellular coverage without having to build its entire ground infrastructure from scratch.

That would offer Musk a potential shortcut into the estimated $235B U.S. wireless market.

The idea is to combine Starlink's satellite coverage with traditional cellular networks, which remain essential in densely populated cities where direct-to-satellite connections are less efficient.

SpaceX also recently agreed to acquire roughly $8B in additional wireless spectrum to support its mobile ambitions.

However, Boost's existing network agreements may not automatically transfer to SpaceX, meaning AT&T and T-Mobile could still need to approve access.

Talks remain ongoing, and no deal has been reached.

🚨 BREAKING: Hackers are hitting supermarket freezers in 5 countries at the same time.

This is what Covid looked like in week 1. A few countries. Small numbers. Nobody called it a crisis.

1/ Sweden: stores say hackers hit their cooling overnight. One says fridges and freezers were set to 50°C, and the food spoiled. ICA Kvantum stores in Sjöbo and Tomelilla were hit, plus at least 6 Coop stores. Sjöbo stayed closed through the morning, threw out all affected goods and apologized. ICA says it is working to restore normal operations. In Sankt Olof a store manager said "everything is ruined." Sweden's National Cybersecurity Centre is working on several incidents.

2/ Estonia: the CEO of cooling firm Kitman Coldtech says several clients were targeted and a large chain's freezer was raised to +50°C. It was found and addressed in about 10 minutes, no major damage.

3/ Ireland: SuperValu pulled ALL fresh and frozen food from 13 stores. Its owner, Musgrave, confirmed a "cybersecurity incident" on a "specific model" of fridge.

4/ Luxembourg: Ahold Delhaize says an "IT incident" hit fridges and freezers at dozens of its supermarkets across Luxembourg and Belgium.

5/ Belgium: more than 40 Delhaize, at least 15 Carrefour and around 5 Spar stores were hit. Cold storage climbed to 15°C. Aisles were closed off and large amounts of stock were destroyed. A notice at one Proxy Delhaize said its systems had "fallen victim to hacking."

Now zoom out.

A freezer normally sits at -18°C. In Estonia, hackers reportedly got in through older controllers. In France, the controller maker said many devices were obsolete or ran outdated firmware. Raise the temperature overnight and the food rots. "You can't unspoil food," one professor said.

It did not start today. 3 weeks ago hackers raised freezers at more than 350 sites in France to as high as 50°C. There were fires. Intermarché's CEO put the cost at "tens of millions of euros nationwide in a single day." Sources suspect Russian involvement there. No group has claimed it. That same day an analyst said Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium were affected too.

Covid emptied the shelves. Nobody is calling this a crisis yet. But the Financial Times already puts the ruined food at millions of euros.

Officials say the Pentagon is treating late-August freezer failures on US military bases as a suspected hack. At least 6 base stores were hit. Army investigators are working with French law enforcement.

5 countries in one day. 11 countries named since August.

$MRVL TO ACQUIRE $LITE IN $115B ALL-STOCK DEAL

Marvell has agreed to acquire Lumentum in an all-stock transaction valued at approximately $115B in enterprise value, combining two major suppliers of AI infrastructure and optical networking technology.

Under the agreement:

• Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each LITE share, implying roughly $1,132 per share.

• The offer represents a 23.9% premium to unaffected closing prices on October 28.

• Marvell shareholders will own approximately 67% of the combined company, with Lumentum shareholders holding 33%.

The deal brings together Marvell's custom AI chips, networking switches and interconnect technology with Lumentum's lasers, optical transceivers and optical circuit switching capabilities.

The bigger opportunity is the growing shift from copper to optical connectivity as AI data centers require faster data transfer, greater bandwidth and improved power efficiency.

Marvell says the combination could expand its addressable market to $550B, allowing it to offer more integrated connectivity solutions across AI data centers and within advanced chip packages.

The companies also expect:

• More than $1B in annual run-rate cost synergies.

• Improved long-term revenue growth and profit margins.

• Accretion to Marvell's adjusted EPS in the first year after closing.

Matt Murphy will remain CEO of the combined company, with the transaction expected to close in H1 2028, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals.

Separately, Marvell reaffirmed the midpoint of its fiscal Q3 revenue guidance while narrowing the expected range to ±2% from ±5%.

Following the Lumentum / Marvell deal: 

My opinion is that independent Western laser players, like $AAOI, $COHR, and $SIVE became a lot more strategically valuable. 

$MTSI and $SMTC should get some attention too as emerging laser players in 2027. 

If I had to guess: 

1. Companies competing against Marvell, or not in the $NVDA ecosystem bandwagon, such as $AMD, are likely going to rethink their relationship with $LITE.

If getting bottlenecked by Nvidia capacity agreements wasn't enough... Incentives around qualifying + bringing up other laser players, seems very necessary now. 

Since you generally don't want competitors like Marvell to have influence or visibility over your roadmaps, IP, capacity, pricing, etc. even if there is a "firewall".  

2. $MRVL acquiring Lumentum opened pandoras box in a way of acquiring a critical chokepoint all your competitors + buyers use. 

$LITE was used by your major hyperscalers and across AI supply chains. 

Now, your leaders might wonder if weaponizing capacity agreements might not be as effective.... If someone else can just buy the entire company. 

There's only a few major public merchant Western players out there, and I'm also sure many others will want to follow the Marvell / Broadcom route via vertical integration, given I think $MRVL saves around $1B+ in costs/year. 

So M&A premiums likely went up. 

$SMTC was actively looking to buy laser capacity via M&A so I'm sure they're looking at $SIVE given their 100M CW DFB laser expansion + tiny MC. 

$JBL also probably wants to vertically integrate down the road too so $SIVE is also an acquisition target for their 1.6T program. 

$AMD was looking for ELSFP + CW capacity given Nvidia bottlenecks, so I'm sure they've looked at $AAOI. 

can go on and on about other ASIC players (like in Taiwan) that likely are looking at vertical integration too.

Since multiple players use a small subset of laser suppliers, if competitors just go ahead and buys them... 

There's a lot pressure to M&A for their own supply chain defensibility. 

TLDR: Independent laser suppliers should capture a material strategic revaluation since $MRVL + $LITE, sets a new precedent + implications. 

We'll see what happens.

Legendary Winnie the Pooh and Tigger Voice Actor, Jim Cummings, Celebrates His 74th Birthday! 🎂🎙️

Few voices have brought as much joy to generations of animation fans as Jim Cummings. Best known for voicing Winnie the Pooh and Tigger, he has kept the Hundred Acre Wood's most beloved characters alive with Pooh's gentle warmth and Tigger's boundless energy. His unmistakable performances have become a treasured part of countless childhood memories.

With a career spanning hundreds of productions, Cummings has also brought to life Darkwing Duck, Pete, Dr. Robotnik, Taz, and Hondo Ohnaka. From Disney classics and Saturday morning cartoons to Star Wars and video games, his incredible vocal range has made him one of animation's most recognizable talents.

He was also the singing voice behind Lion King's Scar! As well as being the substitute voice actor of various iconic characters like Shredder from TMNT.

Some of his most iconic voice roles include:
• Winnie the Pooh — Winnie the Pooh
• Tigger — Winnie the Pooh
• Scar — The Lion King (Singing Voice)
• Darkwing Duck / Negaduck — Darkwing Duck
• Pete — Goof Troop / Mickey Mouse Franchise
• Dr. Ivo Robotnik — Sonic the Hedgehog (1993)
• Tasmanian Devil / Taz — Taz-Mania / Looney Tunes
• Hondo Ohnaka — Star Wars: The Clone Wars / Rebels
• Cat — CatDog
• Shredder — Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (Substitute)
• Ed the Hyena — The Lion King
• Ray the Firefly — The Princess and the Frog
• Don Karnage — TaleSpin
• Bonkers D. Bobcat — Bonkers
• Fuzzy Lumpkins — The Powerpuff Girls
• King Louie — TaleSpin
• Minsc — Baldur's Gate / Baldur's Gate II
• Fat Cat — Chip 'n Dale: Rescue Rangers
• Monterey Jack — Chip 'n Dale: Rescue Rangers
• Steele — Balto
• Kaa the Snake — The Jungle Book 2 / Jungle Cubs
• Rasputin —  (Singing Voice)

Happy 74th birthday, Jim Cummings! Thank you for giving Winnie the Pooh his comforting voice, Tigger his unforgettable laughter, and so many beloved characters their unique personalities. Your extraordinary talent has filled generations of childhoods with laughter, adventure, and magic. Your voice will forever be a part of animation history! 🎂🎙️❤️
