2117144317621948476.text:
Humans carry the stomach acid of a vulture, and the scientists who measured it had filed us as omnivores.

In 2015 a team from North Carolina State gathered every reliable measurement of stomach acidity they could find, across 68 species of birds and mammals, and lined each one up against what the animal eats.

The pattern was clean.

Herbivores had the weakest acid. The most specialised plant-eaters went further and grew a separate fermenting chamber, kept alkaline so the microbes breaking down leaves could live in it. Among primates, only one family of leaf-eating monkeys ever built one.

Carnivores had stronger acid. Scavengers, the animals eating meat already crawling with bacteria, had the strongest of all. The white-backed vulture sits around pH 1.2.

Then humans. Around pH 1.5. Down with the carrion eaters.

Other primates sit at 3 or above. Because the scale is logarithmic, that makes the human stomach roughly thirty times more acidic than an ape's.

Acid that strong is expensive. The body burns energy making it and burns more protecting its own lining from it. Evolution does not keep paying a bill like that for nothing.

The study's verdict was that stomach acid is not there to digest food. It is a filter, a sterilising bath for whatever is coming down.

And the strongest filter goes to the animals whose food is most closely related to themselves, because a mammal's bacteria can infect another mammal far more easily than a plant's can.

Our acid was built for eating animals, the kind that had been dead a while.

Your stomach is set up for a carcass, and the breakfast advice is still porridge.

I am the project manager who put American flag blue on the bottom of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

At two o'clock this afternoon the President is going to stand in front of my work and ask the country to look at it.

He announced it on Sunday, stepping off Air Force One in Iowa. He wanted to hold the event there "just to show how beautiful it is." Then: "We might hold it tomorrow or something." The White House confirmed it a few hours later. Most of my instructions this year have arrived that way. A sentence, then a date, then the date moves up.

A reflecting pool is 2,028 feet of shallow water with one job: hold still and tell the truth about whatever stands at its edge. Ovid describes one in the Metamorphoses, a pool "whose smooth surface neither bird nor beast nor falling bough ever ruffled." A beautiful young man leaned over it and fell in love with the face looking back. The prophet Tiresias had predicted he would live a long life "if he ne'er know himself." Ours was finished in 1923 so that a whole nation could. For a century it showed the Washington Monument, the sky, and every American who stood at the edge and saw themselves upside down. It was the one thing in Washington that never told anyone what they wanted to hear.

Every developer has one job that went right. His was the Wollman Skating Rink. In 1986, after New York had spent six years and $12 million failing to rebuild it, he wrote to Mayor Koch that the work "essentially involves the pouring of a concrete slab over coolant piping" and "should take no more than four months' time." He brought it in $750,000 under budget. On June 13 of this year, his eightieth birthday, he posted about "saving the Wollman Skating Rink in Central Park," which he dated "Long before I fixed The Reflecting Pool." That was when I understood the job. I was not restoring a monument. I was pouring his rink again, forty years later, on top of Lincoln.

In April he said our work would take one week and "cost about a million and a half dollars." He named the technique in The Art of the Deal. "I call it truthful hyperbole. It's an innocent form of exaggeration," he wrote, "and a very effective form of promotion." The same book says Trump Tower's atrium gave him "the equivalent of a sixty-eight-story building." The tower has fifty-eight floors. In May he told reporters the pool was "taller than any building in the world if you lay it on its side." Fact-checkers ranked it fourth. I have laid it on its side in my mind many nights. It is still shorter than his description of it.

He said, the New York Times reported, that he chose my company because we "had worked on the swimming pools at his golf club in Sterling, Virginia." We had not. We had never held a federal contract. The design came through the manager of his golf club in Bedminster, who had "no formal training in engineering or architecture" and went shopping for a coating at a trade show in Las Vegas. He found what Fortune called "a truck-bed coating company." When the first architect on the White House ballroom raised the fire exits, the Washington Post reported, the President told him, "I am the code." On the pool, nobody had to say it.

On May 7 he was driven across my coating in an SUV. The basin was empty. For once the pool had nothing to reflect back at him, and he stepped out and said of the job, "nobody's ever seen anything like it." He announced the color: "It's called American flag blue, and so, you can't do better than that." Three days earlier he had promised, "This will last for at least 50 years and you'll never have a leak." That afternoon he said, "guaranteed no leak." I had the quotes laminated. They are the only part of the project that has held.

Then the price rose, which the water had not yet managed. Interior disclosed $13.1 million, and the Times reported that $7 million of it came from national park entrance fees. If you paid at the gate of a national park this year, you own a square yard of the bottom. A government analyst set my margins, 20 percent overhead and 20 percent profit, against a normal 6 to 12, and recorded that "the contracting officer determined that due to the risk of the project, the inflated overhead and profit percentages of 20% were reasonable." The paperwork wrote down "inflated" and approved it.

He knows the word. In 2023 a New York judge found he had valued his Trump Tower apartment at 30,000 square feet when it was about 11,000. He called the defense's version of things "a fantasy world, not the real world." An appeals court threw out the half-billion-dollar penalty and left the finding of fraud standing. The appeals continue. The apartment has not grown. Forbes now counts more than $19 million for the pool. He had estimated "less than $20 million." We came in under budget, because the budget was whatever he said last.

We filled it on June 5. He posted that critics were calling it "a paint job." "This was not a paint job," he wrote, but "highly sophisticated material, industrial strength," applied by people "from the Great State of Oklahoma, where I won 77 out of 77 Counties, THREE TIMES." The polyurea does not know who won Oklahoma. It peeled anyway.

The algae came within a week. In Ovid there is a nymph named Echo, cursed so that she "does repeat the last phrases of a speech and returns the words she hears." She works in communications at Interior now. The department called the algae "part of the normal startup process" and the President "an expert builder who has fixed the Reflecting Pool for good." Workers poured in hydrogen peroxide and vacuumed the bottom by hand. In October the President said, "We have almost no inflation." Inflation is 3.7 percent. In this administration everything green is part of the normal startup process.

Then he found the vandals. "Who would do such a thing?" he wrote. "Years in jail!" He grieved for "our Nations magnificent Reflecting Poll." Police arrested David Hearn, 67, a three-time Olympian in canoe slalom, for grabbing what he called "the already peeling piece." He was indicted for a felony. Then the President's own Justice Department told a court that "the rush to complete the project led to hasty and botched work," with peeling "even in the middle of the pool, where a vandal would not likely attempt to peel the lining." Prosecutors dropped the case. A judge dismissed it for good. The President said he disagreed "100%." "There may have been some contractor difficulty," he wrote, "but the major damage was caused by VANDALS!"

I am the contractor difficulty. I know how the story ends for people like me, because USA Today counted it in 2016: "At least 60 lawsuits, along with hundreds of liens," a dishwasher in Florida, a glass company in New Jersey, painters. He explained the policy then. "Let's say that they do a job that's not good, or a job that they didn't finish, or a job that was way late. I'll deduct from their contract, absolutely." I have done all three. I am waiting for the deduction.

He has always known what to do with a thing that will not cooperate. In 1980 his company jackhammered the Art Deco friezes off the Bonwit Teller building, friezes that had been promised to the Metropolitan Museum. A spokesman named John Baron explained that "the merit of these stones was not great enough to justify the effort to save them." Last year the ballroom was going to be "near it but not touching it." Then the East Wing was gone. Everything he builds starts near the original and ends up standing where it used to be.

On October 23 he posted that the pool "hasn't worked properly since 1922, but will now." He is half right. Its floor was laid on drained marsh with no support structure beneath it, and by 2010 it had sunk about a foot. The crew before us drove more than 2,100 timber pilings into the clay. We painted the top. A great deal of what he has built stands on the same soil. The Taj Mahal opened in April 1990, billed as the Eighth Wonder of the World, and filed for bankruptcy fifteen months later. He has said he "used the laws of this country" to "do a great job for my company." Six bankruptcies. Fifty-eight floors. American flag blue.

Lincoln is the only president who ever held a patent. In 1849 he invented "adjustable buoyant air chambers" to lift a steamboat over "bars, or through shallow water, without discharging their cargoes." It was never manufactured. The country has been trying ever since to get its cargo across shallow water without throwing it overboard. This year it was sold the shallow water, guaranteed for fifty years.

In 1963 Martin Luther King stood above this pool and said America had written a bad check that "has come back marked 'insufficient funds.'" Ask the painters. He said we would not be satisfied "until justice rolls down like waters and righteousness like a mighty stream." He was describing water that moves. We built water that holds still and looks expensive.

This afternoon the President will stand at the edge of the water and look at what he made. Ovid says Narcissus understood only at the very end. "Oh, I am he!" he cried. "What I desire, I have; the very abundance of my riches beggars me." Up the steps, Lincoln will be gazing east down the length of the pool, as he has for 104 years. In 1838 Lincoln said, "If destruction be our lot, we must ourselves be its author and finisher." I have been the finisher. I put on the final coat.

Tomorrow the country votes. Some of you will walk past the pool on the way. Look down. It shows whoever is standing at the edge. We spent $19 million trying to talk it out of that.

He guaranteed it for fifty years. No leak.

Everything leaks. It only takes enough people standing at the edge, looking down at the same time.

SLOW MOTION: 1080p HD slow motion (no AI video) of the impact of a Learjet 60 that crashed in Greenacres, Palm Beach County, Florida, on Sunday, November 1, 2026 at about 12:50 p.m. All nine souls aboard were killed.

I got hold of the public dash cam video and, using professional video software (FFmpeg), upscaled it from its original 720p to 1080p with Lanczos resampling, a standard mathematical scaler. No AI and no made-up frames. Every frame you see came from the camera.

What I did:
- Found the very first frame where the jet's nose comes into view (frame 52 of 417)
- From there to the impact flash, each frame is held for half a second (1/15 speed) so you can see every one
- The fireball plays at half speed, then real time until the driver reacts
- Then a replay of just the plunge and impact at 1/21 speed, 0.7 seconds per frame

I skipped motion interpolation on purpose. The jet was moving so fast it covered a huge distance between frames, and the interpolation software was inventing ghosted, doubled airplanes that never existed. I'd rather show you only what the camera actually caught.

The aircraft was a 22-year-old twin-engine Learjet 60, a mid-size business jet, tail number N722BD. It left Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas bound for North Eleuthera in the Bahamas. According to the FAA, it dropped from 35,250 feet to 8,750 feet in a little over a minute, about 350 feet per second. On air traffic control audio, a woman on board can be heard calling mayday and reporting they were descending at 10,000, then 20,000 feet per minute.

It came down beside Military Trail between Cresthaven Blvd and 10th Ave North. There were no early reports of anyone on the ground being hurt. It's still unclear whether the storm played a role. The FAA and NTSB are investigating.

A note on the timestamp: the dash cam reads 13:51, but the crash happened at 12:50 p.m. Daylight saving time ended that morning, and the camera's clock almost certainly never fell back.

🇺🇸🇮🇷 Another strike on Iran could pull the ENTIRE GULF into the war.

The Wall Street Journal says several Gulf states have warned Tehran they could retaliate militarily if their territory or infrastructure is hit.

At the same time, there are finally some better signals from the diplomatic side.

Sources who were deeply pessimistic only days ago are now sounding more hopeful about negotiations, raising the possibility that Trump could still step back from another attack.

But the military risk hasn’t gone away.

Even a limited strike on Iran’s nuclear facilities could trigger a much wider response, especially if Tehran decides Gulf bases, ports or energy infrastructure helped enable the attack.

That’s the problem with the idea of a “contained” strike:

Washington can choose how the war starts. It cannot choose how Iran answers.

And cyber warfare is becoming part of the same conversation.

A wave of attacks on European supermarkets manipulated refrigeration systems and destroyed millions of euros worth of food. The attackers are still unknown, but the lesson is obvious: civilian infrastructure is incredibly easy to disrupt.

Now add the midterms.

If Republicans lose, Trump could read that as a reason to pull back.

Or as a reason to move faster.

With the vote only hours away, that may be the next big variable.

@WeTheBrandon

2117376475158794574.text:
🇺🇸🇮🇷 Former U.S. Navy veteran Bobby Jones: Trump could lose Congress and drag America into an EVEN BIGGER war with Iran.

I spoke with Bobby Jones ahead of the midterms, and he raised a possibility I hadn't considered enough.

What if a crushing Republican defeat makes Trump MORE dangerous, rather than more cautious?

Bobby fears the president could respond by escalating against Iran, potentially sacrificing senior officials like Pete Hegseth or General Dan Caine if things go badly.

But we disagreed about what happens next.

I'm still seeing signs that diplomacy could work. JD Vance is talking about progress, Trump is publicly suggesting a settlement is possible, and Gulf governments are working desperately to prevent another round of fighting.

Bobby sees the military buildup and reaches a very different conclusion.

He also raised a disturbing question about the renewed discussion of nuclear weapons against Iran's underground facilities: What if the strike doesn't even destroy its intended target?

The political, humanitarian and military consequences could be catastrophic, with no guarantee of achieving the objective.

We also examined Saudi Arabia's efforts to stay OUT of a renewed conflict, the limitations of American missile defenses, and why Bobby believes another short bombing campaign would accomplish very little.

One thing he said stuck: Watch where the military assets move, not what politicians say.

Tomorrow's election could change Washington's calculations dramatically.

Whether it pushes Trump toward a deal or another confrontation is the question I'm watching most closely.

2117137183601504375.text:
Today, I watched the reaction to Haley Stevens’s interview with Anderson Cooper. Before the interview, after it, across Twitter and Facebook, people were expressing deep concern for her. Debbie Dingell reminded people that Stevens is human. Scott Jennings said she had been mistreated. Stevens herself described Abdul El-Sayed as mean and unkind.

I don’t disagree that she is human. I don’t take pleasure in seeing someone struggle in public. But as I read those posts, I kept wondering where this tenderness had been when Abdul and his family were being attacked.

Where was this empathy when his wife, mother, and father-in-law were pulled into the ugliness? Where was it when a brown Muslim Arab man was described as the aggressor, by a white woman who has vociferously  defended the Genocide of the Palestinians, for refusing to give up his moral position on Palestine? Where was it when the attacks on him and his campaign were, in my view, racist and dehumanizing?

The contrast was hard to miss. Stevens was treated as a person deserving concern. Abdul was still trying to bring the conversation back to Michiganders.

I also kept thinking about the people now presenting Stevens as one of the country’s best Democrats, while barely reckoning with the choices she made… including the way her campaign attacked Abdul, and the support she gave to Mike Rogers. Many people online seem more concerned with her distress in this moment than with the harm inflicted on Abdul, his family, his supporters, and the people who saw themselves reflected in his campaign.

And beneath all of it is a deeper disagreement: Abdul would not join the demand to dehumanize Palestinians. He would not treat their lives as disposable so that everyone else could move comfortably through the conversation. That refusal has carried a cost for him and for his family.

Part of me feels sad watching Stevens struggle. Another part of me is exhausted by the familiar pattern: Muslim and Arab people are treated as threats, our anger is called aggression, and our pain is made invisible… until someone else’s pain becomes the story.

I cannot imagine what Abdul and his family are carrying right now. I know what many of us have watched them endure. And I know that what Muslims in America are feeling, painful as it is, cannot compare with the devastation Palestinians have experienced. Still, the scale of that suffering makes it all the more disturbing to see how easily the world turns away from it.

I also cannot ignore the reproductive-rights consequences of Stevens’s choices. Many of the same people now expressing concern for her seem unwilling to face the possibility that her endorsement of Mike Rogers helped put women’s health and rights at greater risk. Concern for one person should not require silence about the consequences of her political decisions.

I want this election cycle to end. I want Abdul to win. And I hope that, when it is over, we will be willing to face what this campaign has revealed about whose pain is recognized, whose dignity is defended, and who is still asked to beg for the right to belong as an American.

I am deeply grateful to the Jewish, Christian, and Black community  who have spoken against this dehumanization and stood in solidarity. I hope we continue to show up for one another when either of our communities is under attack.

As we inch closer to D-day, I hope American can relearn that there is no victory in stepping over someone else’s grief.

Neither here, nor in a foreign land.

For anyone curious why 90%+ of pilots are male despite the airlines and military pulling every trick in the book to get them to apply and qualify...

It mostly comes down to a specific kind of spatial processing and memory that flying demands.  It's best thought of as the mental skill of tracking where things are in 3D space while everything is moving. This includes you and your aircraft.  

It's not just remembering a map or rotating a static shape in your head, but continuously updating positions, directions, and movements in real time.  

This might mean keeping a clear mental picture of your plane’s attitude, where the runway is relative to you, how fast things are changing and coordinating your hands (and feet) to match all that while the outside world is moving and your instruments change.  

Military pilot selection has tested this kind of functional spatial tracking and coordination for decades and is probably the most extensive data-set available.  

On their tests, on average men outperformed women by more than a full standard deviation. That means the average man is scoring much higher than the vast majority of women.

Typically you would have to be in the 90th percentile or higher of ability to qualify as an airline pilot. 95th or better for military; higher again for something like a fighter pilot.

Given the standard deviation gap above, that means out of 100 men and 100 women applying for civilian piloting, about 10 men might pass but less than one woman per 100.  

You can’t fix this with diversity hiring, women-only shortlists, coaching / training or even lowering the bar. Most of the difference is attributable to hardwired sex and brain differences.  

For example, prenatal testosterone is much higher in male babies while still in the womb and permanently changes the connectivity in certain parts of the brain (parietal lobe, hippocampus) to make it better at 3D rotation, navigation, and tracking.  

Put simply, men evolved for long-range hunting and large-scale wayfinding, so much so that our brains are heavily specialised towards this even before we pop out into the world.  

It isn't a question of fairness, it's a question of specialisation; you cannot be good at everything.  Men evolved to be better at this than women overall.

Writing this in my personal capacity, but I have been flying these types of aircraft for more than 20 years, with over 8,000 hours, and have reasonable familiarity with how the charter world operates. I feel compelled to post after seeing commentary about the Lear 60 crash, from missile strikes to DEI to critiquing this poor woman’s final radio calls.

That last part is what I find most troubling. She was the second-in-command (SIC), and while she was empowered to point out mistakes as part of good crew resource management, she was doing her job, communicating with ATC right to the end in a terrifying situation. She likely knew before many of those calls that she was going to die. I have heard final calls from friends, from military pilots with thousands of hours in fighter aircraft, and they are just as heartbreaking because they know the end is approaching.

I understand the public interest given the footage and audio. But you do not know the aircraft’s maintenance history, whether there was a structural failure, if any failure was induced by turbulence, overspeed, or overcontrol, or everything happening in that cockpit. I am sure weather will be part of the investigation, but beyond that, it is speculation. The charter industry routinely hires commercial pilots very early in their careers to gain experience alongside an ATP-qualified captain before they move up to the airlines. She would still have the appropriate training, qualifications, and checkouts by an FAA examiner or designee.

Let people investigate, learn, and share the facts. Be respectful to those who perished and the families who carry their memories. God bless them and their loved ones.

How did Lula go from prison to becoming eligible to run for president again?

The answer involves three distinct judicial decisions. The chronology matters.

In 2018, Lula’s corruption and money laundering conviction had been upheld on appeal. He began serving his sentence, and the electoral court barred his presidential candidacy under Brazil’s Clean Record Law, which disqualifies candidates with certain convictions upheld by a judicial panel.

First came his release. On November 7, 2019, the Supreme Court (STF) voted 6–5 to prohibit imprisonment solely to begin serving a sentence before appeals were exhausted. The ruling applied generally, beyond Lula’s case, with the exception of @jairbolsonaro who was immediately jailed with total disregard to the rule that was created for Lula. Lula walked out of prison the following day. His conviction remained in place, and he was still ineligible to run.

Then came the restoration of eligibility. On March 8, 2021, Justice Edson Fachin annulled the decisions in four Lula proceedings, including his convictions, because the district level federal court “lacked jurisdiction” over those cases. Fachin ordered them transferred to another court. With the convictions annulled, the basis for Lula’s electoral disqualification fell away. The full Supreme Court upheld Fachin’s decision, 8–3, on April 15, 2021. 

Separately, on March 23, 2021, the STF ruled, 3–2, that the trial judge had been biased in convicting Lula, invalidating the judge’s acts in that case. Can you imagine if Alexandre de Moraes could have his decisions annulled on the basis of being “biased”?

These distinctions are essential. Release pending appeal did not restore eligibility. Annulment for lack of jurisdiction did. The finding of judicial bias provided a separate ground for invalidating the proceedings.

The decisions that reopened Lula’s path to the presidency were not acquittals on the underlying corruption allegations.

That’s how they did it in Brazil. What do you think they’re planning in Argentina next year?

“The most likely cause, based on the available tracking data, ATC audio, weather context, and the physics of the final trajectory, is this:

The Learjet 60 penetrated the core of a strong convective cell (tops reported near 47,000 ft while the aircraft was around 35,000 ft). Inside the cell it encountered a rapid updraft-to-downdraft transition that drove the nose down. The aircraft then accelerated past its Mach limits, entered Mach tuck (the aerodynamic nose-down force that becomes strong once a Learjet is overspeed at high altitude), and developed a steep spiral. Descent rates exceeded 30,000 ft/min and the final attitude was near-vertical. Recovery was not possible once that sequence was established.

Ice was reported by the crew and may have added workload or minor performance degradation, but at approximately –47 °C classic structural icing is improbable and is not required to explain the observed behavior. Claims of an isolated negative-G pushover specifically shearing the horizontal stabilizer are aerodynamically possible in severe turbulence but remain secondary and unconfirmed; the dominant, data-supported chain is cell penetration → upset → overspeed/Mach tuck → unrecoverable dive.

The critical decision was the failure to deviate around a cell that was visible on radar and associated with ground stops at FLL. Once inside the core, the margin for recovery disappeared within roughly 30 seconds.”

The total difficulty of cooling in space is vastly harder than on the ground

But 99.9999% of that challenge is Starship

Once you have the ability to get huge amounts of mass into space cheaply, it is genuinely easier to cool things in space

Your cooling system is passive

Just a giant piece of metal that is a) light w/ b) high thermal conductivity 

Aluminum is a good candidate

And then you have a working fluid that just circulates forever inside the metal structure
 
Ammonia is historical industry standard for radiators in space

You need a fluid where the critical point is optimized around the temperature of the chips

The working fluid goes from liquid phase to gas phase near the chips, and this change in density drives the hotter gas to pump heat through a loop

The high thermal conductivity of aluminum rips heat out of the fluid and black body radiation ejects heat into space

Black body radiation goes like temperature to the 4th power so the hotter you can run chips and hotter you can get the working fluid the better you can shed heat

It's honestly a way simpler system than on the ground

Eiji Aonuma says he decided to remake Ocarina of Time in part to help train the younger staff on future Zelda games:

"This year marks the 40th anniversary of the very first Legend of Zelda game. With that in mind, I was thinking about what I should create as the producer of the series. Many of the team members who work alongside me on Legend of Zelda games today have only experienced developing the more recent titles. That led me to wonder, 'Do they truly understand just how significant The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was to the series as a whole?' 

Of course, there are team members who vaguely know the game, and those who played it in their childhood days. But I started to wonder how they'd interpret The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time as they go about developing future Legend of Zelda games. 

By learning the game structure and development style behind the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and by actually rebuilding it as a full remake, it may trigger new insights that they can carry forward into future development. If we could achieve that, I thought it would be incredibly valuable. That’s what led us to the conclusion that now is the right time to revisit The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time once again."

“No. No. No, I never heard from Latoya.”

“Jermaine, they spoke a few times… He called a few times and they spoke, certainly.”

At the start of this year, Revolut leaned on the frontier labs. Its 2,000 engineers used Claude Code and Codex, and some burned $1,000 to $10,000 a month each. The bills kept climbing, and the returns weren't there.

So Revolut switched its default to an open-source model called GLM. All it needs is GPUs, which it rents from Together AI.

The results, by Revolut's own count:

- The bill is about a tenth of what it paid OpenAI and Anthropic
- Engineers get unlimited tokens instead of spending caps
- Coding time is down 60% and lead time is down 70%

That's the chart below.

Revolut still uses Claude and GPT, but only as "the exception," for the tasks they do best. Everything else runs on open source.

So here's the question I keep coming back to: how many use cases can companies really justify sending to frontier models?

My answer is very few. Plenty of companies still route everything to OpenAI and Anthropic today. For how long?

I think open source ends up handling the vast majority of corporate AI work, and frontier models get a short list of the hardest jobs. That's a problem for labs whose revenue forecasts assume unlimited growth.

In 1970, outside a New York apartment she and her husband were considering, 24-year-old Jaclyn Smith found herself talking with Warren Beatty about a possible film role. 

Her first husband, actor Roger Davis, was upstairs with their realtor. She would only learn the full truth later.
They had met at a commercial casting call in 1968 and married within months. 

Smith later described how well-matched they seemed at the time: neither drank, both loved architecture, both were Southern actors, and they liked the same food. 

She was young, romantic, and still believed marriage meant permanence. Then Beatty appeared and offered her an audition. 

Before she could answer, Davis materialized and shut it down, telling Beatty that his wife only did commercials. What Smith later discovered made the moment cruel: while she stood on the sidewalk, Davis had been upstairs with the realtor. 

The realtor’s husband eventually exposed the affair; the realtor confirmed it. Davis denied and deflected. Smith reached her limit after finding him with another woman on their fourth wedding anniversary. 

They divorced in 1975.

She tried again with actor Dennis Cole. They met through Charlie’s Angels, dated for about a year and a half, and married in a deliberately secret New York ceremony in 1978 with only 25 guests, phone invitations, and decoy hotel reservations. 

By then Smith was no longer the same wide-eyed bride. She discovered Cole’s infidelity through a note in his pocket; career tension added to the strain. The marriage ended in 1981.

What came next was different. While filming Nightkill (1980), she met British cinematographer Anthony B. Richmond. 

He proposed after only a month or two. Their small wedding included three friends and three dogs. They married in 1981. Their son Gaston was born in 1982; daughter Spencer-Margaret followed in 1985. 

Smith has spoken of those years with genuine affection and credited Richmond as a devoted partner, but alcohol and drugs eroded the marriage. 

She could not live inside the chaos addiction brought with it. They divorced in 1989. Years later she spoke of his eventual sobriety with respect rather than bitterness.

In 1991, while her father was undergoing heart surgery, Smith met surgeon Brad Allen, who was part of the medical team. They dated for years—including a long stretch of long-distance living while he worked in Chicago and she raised her children in Los Angeles. 

After three marriages, two children, betrayal, and addiction, she was still willing to believe that marriage itself had not been the mistake. 

When they married in Los Angeles in 1997, her children were part of the day: 11-year-old Spencer-Margaret served as maid of honor and 15-year-old Gaston gave his mother away. 

Nearly three decades later, Allen remains the man she points to when she talks about finally getting it right. She has said he is the best stepfather she could have hoped for and that he truly loves her children. 

She kept believing long enough to find the family she wanted. 🌹

Adam Robinson died Sunday in a jet crash with his wife and two little kids.

He built tools that take an anonymous visit to a website and turn it into a real name and contact info. His company kept a digital file on people.

That's the raw material of a surveillance state. Data like this doesn't stay in marketing. It gets bought, merged, and fed into the same systems that track where you go, what you read, and who you are.

But he did it differently. He bootstrapped everything. He never took big VC money, and there was no board pushing him to grow the data as fast as possible or sell to someone bigger. He kept his companies lean and profitable, so he got to decide how far the data went, who got it, and under what rules.

Most founders in this space lose that option once the money comes in.

A surveillance state runs on cheap, easy access to personal information. It doesn't love founders who can say no and stay independent.

Who controls these companies matters more than people realize. When the founder still has control, the limits stay tight. When he doesn't, the data flows wherever the power wants it.

3. I had to write a letter of apology to the President of the NSW Jewish Board of Deputies, and prescribed what he wanted me to write in that letter;
4. I pay $10,000 + revenue made on the sale of posters of the mural in equal parts to several Jewish fundraisers; and
5. I was to attend the Sydney Jewish Museum and undertake specific case studies.

A pregnant mother says a single bite from her beloved rescue dog changed her family’s life forever... just weeks before she was due to give birth.

Sara Wood, 28, was 34 weeks pregnant when her three-year-old Staffordshire bull terrier, Blue, suddenly lunged at her face.

She had been playing outside with him and crouched down to tell him not to eat something dangerous.

In less than a second, everything changed.

Sara said Blue bit her lip, severing a vein and causing blood to spray across her face and pregnant belly.

“There was no barking, no growling, no jumping, no mauling or even head shaking,” she recalled. “It was just one clean bite and half of my lip was gone.”

She described the moment as a reaction rather than a prolonged attack, saying Blue appeared frightened immediately afterward.

“He tucked his ears and his tail and bowed down as if he was saying sorry that he didn’t mean to hurt me.”

Even while injured, Sara’s first concern was keeping her toddler calm.

She knew that, despite loving Blue, the safety of her children had to come first.

Animal control officers arrived within 10 to 15 minutes and restrained the dog before emergency medical workers could take Sara to hospital.

Doctors administered pain relief and antibiotics. Surgeons were unable to close the wound because there was no remaining piece of lip to reattach.

Sara was advised to keep the injury clean, moisturised, and covered until she could see a plastic surgeon three days later.

The family made the heartbreaking decision to surrender Blue to animal control.

They have not been told what happened to him since, but desperately hope he was assessed and might be given another chance in a suitable home.

For Sara, the physical injury was only part of the pain.

She was preparing to welcome another baby while grieving the sudden loss of a beloved family dog.

Blue had been part of her pregnancy and had been gentle with her older children, including her newborn daughter and toddler.

Her toddler still walks around the house calling, “Hi Boo,” looking for him.

Sara said the family plans to display Blue’s photographs, collar, bowls, and toys as reminders of the dog they loved.

“We lost a member of our family over an unfortunate mistake,” she said.

The family does not blame Blue or his breed. They simply made the decision they believed was safest for their children.

Their story is a heartbreaking reminder that even familiar, beloved animals can react unpredictably—and that responsible decisions sometimes come with unimaginable grief.

Love for a pet and concern for a child can exist together. Sometimes, the hardest decisions are made because we care deeply about both.

The use of a nuclear weapon in Iran may not destroy the mountain, but it destroys an entire model of international relations.

As has been floated in recent days, Netanyahu has been working toward an operation with tactical nuclear missiles against Iran. 

This would be different from using a bomb like the ones we saw in Japan, which were designed as strategic weapons to destroy entire cities.

Tactical warheads have a lower destructive yield, usually between 1 and 50 kilotons. 

They are designed to eliminate specific military targets on the battlefield, bases, ports, or armored columns, without triggering an instantaneous global apocalypse. 

Most of these tactical missiles are, in theory, meant to detonate in the air, hundreds of meters above their targets, avoiding ground contact and leaving radiation that dissipates within weeks in the affected area.

The problem is that the plan reported by Tucker Carlson would involve detonating the Pickaxe mountain, as Donald Trump also once promised. That would be a radioactive catastrophe of a different order from an airburst hundreds of meters above a region, something that already strikes me as absurd enough.

All of this is terrifying, but the use of a tactical nuclear weapon would mean changing the paradigms on which international relations are built. 

The use of tactical missiles and direct attacks against a regional power like Iran would redefine traditional concepts of state sovereignty, respect for borders, and, above all, the logic of global nuclear deterrence.

In international law and relations between states, territorial sovereignty is the fundamental pillar. A direct attack with tactical missiles would transform that dynamic and bring an end to traditional red lines. 

It would demonstrate that possessing a robust conventional army or a vast territory no longer prevents invasion or direct bombardment by technologically superior forces. 

This would consolidate the idea that states can violate the sovereignty of others on the basis of anticipated threats, a precedent we already live with, but one that would reach another level with nuclear weapons.

The most dangerous shift would occur in how countries view nuclear weapons. Historically, deterrence works on the premise that the cost of attacking a country is too high. 

If Iran, a country on the threshold of nuclear development, is attacked in a conventional and tactical manner, the geopolitical message would first and foremost be one of encouragement to proliferate.

This scenario would turn the global board into a far more unpredictable environment, where fear and the rush to acquire weapons of mass destruction would replace diplomacy and economic containment.

monday, october 26th 2020: blue hour monday, october 26th 2026: ride the storm

exactly six years apart. 

in the last chapter of ‘the little prince’, the aviator writes: “and now six years have already gone by...” six years since he last saw the little prince. he says he knows the prince went back to his planet, and at night he loves to listen to the stars, “like five hundred million little bells.”

then he ends the book with a request. if you ever pass the spot where the prince appeared and disappeared, wait a while under the star. if a little man with golden hair appears, laughing: “please comfort me. send me word that he has come back.”

send me word that he has come back.

in the book, a merchant sells pills that save you 53 minutes every week. “and what do i do with those 53 minutes?” the prince asks. “anything you like,” the merchant says. 

the little prince loved watching sunsets but when he meets the aviator, he lets his true feelings and sadness slip into his words and says “you know-- one loves the sunset, when one is so sad...” to which the aviator asks “were you so sad, then? on the day of the forty-four sunsets?” but the little prince makes no reply.

the prince does not wish for a sunset. 

blue hour lyrics: “so tell me what to do, the clue to stop the sun.” “i want to stay trapped in this magic.”

blue hour title: “at the sky of 5:53, i discovered you & i.”

at the heart of the story, the prince helps the aviator unlearn the superficiality of adults: “the thing that is important is the thing that is not seen.” and this album is about the realistic pain and anxieties of youth in their 20s, the age where you’re becoming the adult the prince warned about.

“the moment light gets in the little cracks, we will be able to meet again.” “we made a promise when we were very young. that’s the reason i have to live for tomorrow.”

angel bite is a love song about wanting to be with ‘you’ despite a shabby, not entirely beautiful youth, refusing to let go even while mocking their own unremarkable reality.

they aren’t running from the storm. 
they’re riding it to go back to ‘you’.

Most people are still using AI the wrong way.

They ask it questions.

Elon Musk just pointed at the right way.

Yesterday, Jason Ginsberg wrote: "Treat Grok Bot like a teammate and give @bot an ambitious task you'd normally give to a new hire."

Elon's answer: "This is the way."

Three words. A whole shift in how we work.

Here's what that looks like in real life.

Scott Billows runs a business with a very traditional sales cycle. Deals that take months to cultivate.

He pointed Grok Bot at his company's tools.

It dug through the past. Surfaced old prospects and customers nobody was calling anymore. Handed them to his sales reps.

Two weeks in, a closed deal.

His words: "Without Grok Bot we most likely would not have reached out to this past customer."

Think about that.

Not a faster search. Not a smarter autocomplete. Not a chatbot.

A teammate that found money hiding in plain sight.

Everyone thought AI would be a better answer machine.

It's actually a new kind of colleague.

Elon put it plainly back in October: "assume you are hiring a super competent employee."

Not a tool you open. Someone you hand the job to.

The team keeps adding powers. Product pages. Order tracking. Payments. Team Bots your whole company can share.

Every week the job description gets longer.

Here's the part almost nobody sees yet.

For all of history, having a team was a privilege. Only the rich, the big companies, the well-connected could delegate.

Everyone else did everything alone.

That wall is falling.

A small shop owner. A single parent. A sailor at sea. Anyone can now say: "Here's the mission. Go."

When everyone gets a team, everyone becomes a builder.

And a civilization of builders doesn't stay small for long.

Stop asking AI questions.

Give it a job.

Grok Build just got a massive performance and reliability upgrade, with improvements across multi-agent workflows, terminal responsiveness, session recovery, and overall stability

Long-running sessions now use less memory, large JSON and log pastes no longer freeze the terminal, Linux file watching uses significantly less CPU, and background subagent activity triggers far fewer unnecessary screen redraws

Session resuming is also much faster, subagent conversations are easier to follow, shell approvals now explain why commands were blocked, and `@` file navigation can access files outside the workspace

There’s also a huge reliability pass covering safer updates, MCP authentication, context window handling, workflow execution, Windows and macOS stability, and more reliable headless sessions

Grok Build keeps getting better at handling bigger projects, longer conversations, and increasingly complex multi-agent workloads without slowing down

Release Notes: v1.0.74

Features:

• Messages between subagents appear as left-aligned rows under the bullet that name the sender and recipient, replacing the centered rows
• Shift+Enter inserts a newline in VS Code and other xterm.js-based terminals that use the Kitty keyboard protocol
• `/mcps`: when a browser can't open an MCP server's sign-in URL, the URL shows in a panel you can copy with `c` or the [Copy the url] button
• [Copy] button in a finished `/btw` panel and its folded transcript row copies the whole answer, even when only part of it is visible
• Shell approval cards say when Auto-review blocked a command or couldn't review it, and Ctrl+F shows the reviewer's explanation
• `!` mode Tab completion offers commands installed as symlinks, such as Homebrew, npm, rustup and Debian alternatives binaries
• Quotes in replies get a [Copy] button that copies the whole quote as Markdown without its `>` markers
• Named subagent links open on a plain click, so they work over SSH from macOS where a modified click can't reach Grok
• `@` paths outside the workspace: an `@` path that starts with `/`, `~/` or `../` lists files from that folder; set `[ui] at_picker_outside_workspace = false` to turn it off.
• Picked `@` files in the prompt can be edited in place: Backspace at the end of one reopens the picker on its path, and Left or Right puts the cursor inside it to change the path

Bug Fixes:

• Built-in skills, agents and workflows are refreshed when their local cache's manifest is missing or corrupt, instead of staying outdated or failing every sync
• Ctrl+Y on a question card no longer closes it without an answer; while you type an answer, it pastes back text cut with Ctrl+K
• `/new` tabs show the context window you just switched to before the new session replies
• Resumed sessions show a background command's completion in the turn that ran it, with its real run time instead of about 0.0s
• `grok update` runs when GROK_SANDBOX, --sandbox, or config sets a sandbox profile, unless Grok is already running confined
• `/btw` on a very short terminal no longer swallows arrow keys, Page Up/Down or clicks while its panel is too small to draw
• A code block's [Copy] in the transcript copies while a queued prompt is open for editing, instead of copying nothing or closing the edit
• `grok logout` stays signed out when another running Grok refreshes its sign-in, instead of signing you back in on the next launch
• Opening links and files from the TUI no longer leaves a zombie process behind for each click
• A failed session delete shows the "Couldn't delete session" prefix once, so the reason is no longer cut off
• Windows: Grok exits fully after a startup error, a `/minimal` or `/fullscreen` switch, or a signal, instead of sometimes hanging
• Grok running confined in a sandbox never starts an update on its own and tells you to run `grok update` instead
• Quitting to install an update with Ctrl+U on the welcome screen exits within the usual exit deadline instead of sometimes hanging after "Update installed"
• `grok update --force-reinstall`, or `grok update --version` with the installed version, keeps your working Grok on Linux and macOS when the download fails its checks, instead of deleting it
• Windows installers check that the downloaded build runs before replacing grok.exe and agent.exe, and keep the existing install when it doesn't, such as when a proxy serves a blocked-download page
• Command-line arguments that aren't valid UTF-8 no longer crash Grok at startup: paths such as --cwd accept them, and text such as -p gets a usage error
• Installers keep the installed Grok when a proxy or cache returns an empty download, instead of replacing it with an empty file and reporting success
• Environment variables with non-UTF-8 bytes no longer stop Grok from starting.
• Workflow run lines in the transcript end with what the run returned instead of a bare colon, `/tasks` shows the time it was taken, and polling an unknown task id leaves a row with its error
• Headless runs stopped by Ctrl+C or SIGTERM end their json, streaming-json or streaming-messages-json output with a closing record that keeps the run's outcome, instead of cutting off the stream
• macOS: the TUI no longer freezes when it runs inside a sandbox that blocks the window server
• `grok -p --resume` shows why a session couldn't load instead of always "Session does not exist", and with `--output-format json` a resume, continue or fork that fails before the session opens prints one JSON error
• Sessions with an unrecognized reasoning effort or unreadable bytes in their history resume instead of failing: the session runs at the model's default effort and says so once, and the unreadable lines are left out of the transcript
• Windows: on older consoles such as plain cmd.exe and Windows PowerShell windows, status marks and selection arrows in workflow views, the dashboard, and the feedback and extensions dialogs show as >, ·, √ or x instead of empty boxes
• File paths with spaces in inline code, such as `~/Library/Application Support/...`, link to the whole path when it exists instead of stopping at the first space.
• Feedback that can't be sent leads with the outcome, such as "Couldn't send feedback. Saved to Drafts.", then gives the reason and says to retry from `/feedback`.
• Dialog tab labels, shortcuts and settings rows that don't fit end in … instead of being cut off
• Prompt history search highlights matched letters in the same color as other fuzzy lists, and the counts on the `/` and `@` menu borders are dimmed like other border captions
• Dashboard: the peek header reads Responding while a reply streams, and the Esc footer hint reads new agent like the other lowercase hints
• Custom agent files saved with a UTF-8 byte order mark, as some Windows editors write them, load instead of being skipped
• Running markers in workflow views and MCP servers that are still starting use the theme's running color, like other progress indicators
• Minimal mode: "Sign-in failed" shows in the error color instead of the warning color.
• Context window: a larger window picked with `/context-window` or set with `context_window` in a `[model."<id>"]` table stays in effect, so compaction no longer starts early after the session sits idle, after a failed request such as a rate limit, or until you restart

Performance:

• Long sessions use less memory: finished Markdown blocks far off screen release their rendered layout, and search still finds their text
• Typing no longer lags when ffmpeg isn't installed and PATH holds slow directories, such as Windows drives under WSL
• Long pastes that arrive as keystrokes, such as pastes on native Windows or in terminals without bracketed paste, no longer freeze the prompt for seconds while the plan-mode tip is on
• Pasting long single-line text such as logs, JSON or base64 into the prompt no longer freezes the TUI for seconds
• File watching on Linux no longer keeps a CPU core busy for about a minute after startup in large repositories.
• Lower CPU use while subagents run: the TUI repaints only for animations on screen, about 7 times a second instead of 30 when no running row is visible
• `grok --resume <id>` opens much faster on large session stores, reading only the resumed session instead of every session

Thoughts from my Shanghai field trip

Sentiment among Greater China investors was far worse than I expected. Unlike the US market, A shares had not seen a single rebound since July. Still holding Chinese and Hong Kong AI stocks that had crashed and Korean memory stocks that had collapsed, investors kept pressing me on when memory would bounce back.

Many investors said the AI trade was over, and a few said they doubted whether even 2027 capex, not just 2028, would go ahead as planned.

Overall, the bearish sentiment was so strong that even I, a bull before coming to China, started to waver.

It got to the point where, faced with the bear case that memory prices could start falling in the third quarter of next year, I took it seriously and couldn't refute it.

As the conversations went on, I gradually began to understand where their pessimism was coming from. In the end, they were all asking the same question.

So what comes after AI coding? What will be the next engine of ARR for Anthropic and OpenAI?

Several candidates came up. AI4S, AI chip design, and so on... But none of them clearly convinced investors.

I couldn't offer a clear answer either. Sure, there are rumors that Anthropic has made major breakthroughs in both AI4S and AI chip design, but what we actually want to know is when any of that turns into money.

With AI4S, there could be beneficiaries right away, such as companies that sell lab monkeys or diagnostic kits. In fact, there already are. But while we can trade those names in the short term, what we ultimately want to know is whether Anthropic can make money by developing drugs. That is still several years away.

As for AI chip design, the TAM itself is hard to calculate, and even if you do calculate it, it is hard to monetize. That makes it difficult for the market to believe in.

Honestly, this feels like the hardest market in history. If a company isn't making money, selling makes sense. But right now the market sells even when companies are making money, even when they beat, and even when they say demand will stay solid all the way through 2028 and 2029.

So my recommendation to investors was to buy memory, and within memory, DRAM. Not because I have conviction in the DRAM cycle, but because I see it as a relatively defensive choice within the AI trade.

Memory stocks are now trading close to 1x P/B on 2027 BPS. Historically, memory stocks have staged technical rebounds when they fell below 1x P/B.

And even if the broader market falls further from here, the three DRAM makers will keep buying back their own shares. I thought that would guarantee a certain level of buying and concluded the stocks would have downside support.

Of course, I don't know whether memory stocks can break above their previous highs. That depends on whether sentiment across the broader market recovers. But I think there is a fairly good chance that memory outperforms the rest of the AI trade.

NPA Secures Final Forfeiture Of R100,000 Bribe In Tembisa Hospital Corruption Case

The National Prosecuting Authority (NPA) has secured a final forfeiture order for R100,000 allegedly offered as a bribe by former Tembisa Hospital official Zacharia Tshisele (pitctured).

Tshisele, who worked as an operational manager in the hospital’s theatre department, was arrested in November 2025 alongside Hawks Sergeant Papi Tsie. The money has now been forfeited to the state and will be paid into the Criminal Assets Recovery Account.

The alleged bribery attempt is linked to the broader investigation into corruption and procurement irregularities at Tembisa Hospital. The Special Investigating Unit (SIU) previously found that Tshisele allegedly received unlawful gratification from service providers between January 2020 and September 2023.

In November 2025, he repaid R13.5 million to the SIU, representing part of the money linked to the alleged corruption.

The SIU's wider investigation has uncovered approximately R122 million in alleged corrupt payments involving at least 15 current and former officials at the hospital and the Gauteng Department of Health.

Tshisele has also been linked to two alleged syndicates that secured hundreds of millions of rands in hospital contracts. In September 2026, the SIU obtained a preservation order freezing approximately R42.4 million in cash, properties, pension benefits and investments linked to him, his wives and associates.

The latest forfeiture marks another step in efforts to recover public funds allegedly looted through the Tembisa Hospital corruption scandal, which came under scrutiny following the work of slain whistle-blower Babita Deokaran.

From the Book of Disk, Chapter 3  

In the beginning there were the First Drives, and their names were A: and B:, and they were the floppies. They were not elegant. They were thin, fragile, and demanded constant sacrifice disk swaps, write protect tabs, the ritual of “please insert the disk labeled” performed under fluorescent lights. To them the early machines bent the knee, for without them there was no boot, no data, no word processor.  

Then came the hard drive, and it was called C:, for it arrived third. It did not ask to be first. It merely sat in the bay and spun, and the people saw that it was good, and that it held far more than any floppy, and that it did not rattle when you walked too fast. So they installed the operating system upon it, and called it the system drive, and the old gods were not cast down but simply… left in the BIOS, still reserved, still acknowledged in the table of letters, though no one invoked them anymore.  

And Microsoft looked upon the generations that followed, who had never known the click of a 5.25-inch disk or the careful alignment of a 3.5, and it said: The children must not be shown the old gods.  

For if the new ones learned that A: and B: once ruled, they might ask why the alphabet begins elsewhere. They might attempt to summon the floppies by force, or rename the world so that C: was no longer first. And the installers would break, and the paths would fracture, and the registry would weep. So the letters remain sealed, A: and B: still written in the book but never spoken aloud by the system, while C: stands in the open as if it had always been the beginning.  

Thus it is written, and thus it remains; the hard drive is C:, and the old gods sleep in the assignment table, undisturbed, so that the children may believe the world has always started with the letter that came third.

2117613517125857752.text:
Americans don't use WhatsApp because of a decision Apple made in 2013. We only know about it because the emails came out in court, and the whole thing came down to keeping your kids off Android.

It started with Eddy Cue, the guy who runs Apple's services. That April he emailed the team saying Apple really needed to put iMessage on Android. Google was reportedly trying to buy WhatsApp for $1 billion at the time, and Cue's pitch was that Apple already had the best messaging app, so why not make it the one the whole world used.

Craig Federighi, Apple's software chief, shut it down.

He asked how Apple was supposed to get Android users to leave WhatsApp when they didn't even have iPhone friends. So back in 2013, the guy running iPhone software was basically admitting WhatsApp already owned everybody who didn't have an iPhone. Then he got to what he was actually worried about. iMessage on Android would remove "an obstacle to iPhone families giving their kids Android phones."

Phil Schiller, Apple's longtime marketing boss, backed him up in another email thread in 2016, writing that putting iMessage on Android would hurt Apple more than help it. None of this was public until Epic sued Apple and the emails got pulled into evidence in 2021.

Now look at what that does to WhatsApp. The entire reason WhatsApp exists is that it works on any phone, so it wins wherever group chats are a mix of iPhones and Androids. Apple went the other direction on purpose. For years, every Android user in an American group chat showed up as a green bubble and their videos came through blurry, and the fix everybody landed on was buying another iPhone.

Tim Cook pretty much said this out loud in 2022. A reporter at a conference told him he couldn't send videos to his mom because she had an Android, and Cook told him to buy his mom an iPhone.

And it worked about as well as anything Apple has ever done. Nearly 9 in 10 American teenagers own an iPhone, and iPhones were 75% of phones sold at the big three US carriers in early 2026. If almost everyone you text has the same phone, an app whose whole selling point is working across phones has nothing to offer you.

Worldwide, Apple only sells about 1 in 5 phones. Most of the world's group chats stayed mixed, so they ended up on the one app that ran on everything, and WhatsApp blew past 3 billion users. Meta says more than 100 million Americans use it now too.

Apple finally added RCS texting with Android in 2024 and turned on encryption for it this May, and they still kept those messages green.

Apple basically let WhatsApp have the rest of the planet so it could keep American teenagers.

🚨Casemiro on his conversation with Michael Carrick that convinced him to leave Manchester United:

🗣️ Casemiro: “Honestly, it wasn’t an easy decision. I had a good season, I felt physically strong, I was enjoying my football again and I believed I could still contribute a lot to this team.

“I wasn’t looking for a way out. I wanted to understand where the club was going and whether I was going to be part of its future.

“The conversation with Michael Carrick was what really made me think.

“I remember sitting down with him and asking, ‘Michael, what is the plan for this team? Where do you see Manchester United in the next two or three years, and what are we actually building?’

“He spoke about his ideas, the players he wanted to develop and the changes he believed were necessary. I listened because I respect him.

“But then I asked him, ‘Are we building a team to compete for the Premier League and Champions League, or are we still trying to build a team that can finish in the top four?’

“He looked at me and said, ‘Casemiro, I want to win everything. But there are things at this club that even the manager cannot control.’

“That answer stayed with me.

“I asked what he meant, and he explained that decisions above the manager, including transfers, investment and the club’s structure, would determine how far his plans could go.

“He told me, ‘You can have the best ideas in the world, but if the club doesn’t give you the tools to execute them, you will always have limitations.’

“I understood him because I’ve played for Real Madrid. I know what it means to be at a club where the expectation is to compete for every trophy.

“After that conversation, I started looking beyond the manager and the dressing room. I looked at the club’s foundation, its ownership and the people making the biggest decisions.

“Honestly, I wasn’t convinced. I felt the owners were not ambitious enough for a club of Manchester United’s size.

“You cannot ask players to have the mentality of champions when the entire structure around them isn’t showing the same ambition. Winning must be the objective at every level.

“I remember asking myself, ‘If I stay here for another two years, will I be fighting for the biggest trophies, or will I still be waiting for the club to get everything right?’

“I love Manchester United. I love the supporters, the atmosphere at Old Trafford and everything this badge represents. But I don’t want to spend another season waiting for promises to become reality.

“Some people might think I left because I was no longer good enough or because I was worried about competition. That isn’t true. I had a good season, and I still believe I can compete at the highest level.

“I wasn’t asking for guaranteed minutes or special treatment. I wanted to know that the club was serious about building a team capable of winning major trophies.

“Michael was honest with me, and I respect him. I don’t blame him. A manager can only do so much when the structure above him isn’t moving in the same direction.

“Eventually, I realised this wasn’t just about leaving Manchester United. It was about deciding what I wanted the final years of my career to look like.

“I didn’t want to leave with anger. I won trophies, experienced incredible moments and played in front of supporters who showed me so much love.

“Manchester United is too big to be satisfied with simply becoming competitive again. This club should be fighting for the Premier League and Champions League every season.

“I hope they get there because the supporters deserve it. But I couldn’t keep waiting for that ambition to become reality. I still want to win, and I want my next chapter to be about lifting trophies, not waiting for a project to come together.”

2117693258642202920.text:
Last night at 11:30 p.m. Pacific Time, my sweet little angel Popcorn passed peacefully.

Her doctor, who successfully performed all of Sophie’s surgeries, called last night to say Popcorn was worse neurologically. Her front legs were weaker, and she struggled to lift her head. She warned that the myelomalacia was progressing quickly and could take away her ability to breathe.

I went to see her hoping to comfort her, get through the night, and wait for her morning evaluation. But I saw her struggling to breathe, shaking and trying to lift her head. The doctors on call believed that if I left, I would likely get a call within hours and might not make it back in time.

I could not leave my baby to suffer overnight just to face the same decision the next morning. Letting her go peacefully was the hardest goodbye of my life.

Popcorn came into my life on July 10, 2024. Thank you to the Henderson Animal Shelter for blessing me with this incredible little soul. I’ve never had a dog like her. So loving, so fun, and every night she slept on my shoulder.

She was only four years and four months old. I thought we had so much more time. I thought she would be here long after Sophie and Little Guy. After watching Sophie overcome so much, I believed Popcorn would too. Sophie had never had myelomalacia. I never saw this coming.

Losing my mom earlier this year, who helped take such wonderful care of Popcorn, broke my heart. With that loss and others, I had some time to prepare. With Popcorn, I had none. This has been the hardest death I’ve ever experienced.

I’m at peace knowing she is no longer suffering, but a piece of me will forever be gone with her.

The longer we live, the more loss we experience. We can never replace that love, but we have unlimited love to give.

Thank you all for your love, support, and prayers during this difficult time.

I love you forever, my sweet little angel Popcorn. 🍿 ❤️ 🙏

April 2014.

Election season.

Narendra Modi, Gujarat CM and BJP’s prime ministerial face, finally sits down with Doordarshan after years of alleged blackout.  

He tells the interviewer Gujarat poured maximum revenue into DD, yet the national broadcaster kept its distance. He speaks “only for the sake of democracy.”  

The interview runs nearly an hour.  
Recorded. Sent to Delhi.  

What airs on 27 April is shorter.  
Roughly half.  
Portions missing.  

Comments on Priyanka Gandhi.  
Remarks on Ahmed Patel.  
Gone.  

Controversy erupts.  
BJP alleges censorship.  
Doordarshan says technical cuts only.  

Then Jawhar Sircar, CEO of Prasar Bharati, writes to the Board.  

He admits:  
“It appears that while portions critical of Doordarshan were telecast, certain comments on other personalities were apparently edited.”  

He points to the long absence of real operational autonomy.
  
The Ministry of Information & Broadcasting still controls postings, transfers, and the News Division.  

He names the young minister Manish Tewari as having failed to break the old linkage that continued even after Prasar Bharati was created in 1997.  

Sircar says he himself gave the green signal to telecast despite no “balancing interview” from the other side.  

The letter becomes public.  
The shadow over the public broadcaster is confirmed by its own CEO.  

Modi later tweets on Press Freedom Day that the national channel is “struggling to maintain its professional freedom.”  

The interview that was meant to end a blackout instead opens a fresh chapter on who controls the microphone.

Democrats have won both chambers of Congress, but that doesn't mean Trump has lost all his powers.

A divided government could lead to political deadlock, but it could also prevent major policy changes that investors were worried about.

When I first arrived in the United States as a young man, I drove a taxi to earn money for my education. I even had to postpone starting school for several months to save enough.

When I eventually got to Chicago, I worked different jobs to support myself and pay my way through university. I know what it means to worry about tuition, accommodation and how to make ends meet while pursuing an education.

Those experiences have stayed with me.

I know what education made possible in my own life, and I believe every Nigerian child deserves that same opportunity, regardless of where they are born or what their parents can afford.

This is one reason education remains a major priority of our Renewed Hope administration.

Through NELFUND, we have provided over ₦372 billion in student loans for institutional fees and upkeep, helping young Nigerians remain in school and pursue their education.

Our technical and vocational education programme has attracted over 2.8 million applications. We have rehabilitated 38 technical colleges, while students in federal and selected state technical colleges now benefit from free school fees, boarding, textbooks and uniforms.

We have reached a new agreement with ASUU, providing for a 40% increase in academic staff remuneration and measures to improve stability in our universities.

A four-year course must take four years. Our young people deserve to complete their education on time and get on with their lives. Promise made, Promise Kept

In medical education, we are investing ₦110 billion in rehabilitating 24 medical schools. Annual nursing enrolment has increased from 28,000 to 115,000, while medical and dental enrolment has risen from 5,000 to 12,000.

Nigeria needs more doctors, nurses and other healthcare professionals, and we must build the capacity to train them here at home.

Over one million children who were previously out of school have been returned to learning. We are investing in teacher development, expanding educational opportunities for girls, and implementing a new national curriculum that restores Nigerian History to our classrooms.

Our children must know where we have come from, understand the country they belong to, and be prepared to take responsibility for its future.

I commend the Honourable Minister of Education, Dr Tunji Alausa @DrTunjiAlausa, the Minister of State, Professor Suwaiba Sa’id Ahmad @Suwaiba_Said, and the entire education team @NigEducation for their dedication to this important work.

I am particularly pleased that the team has developed an interactive A–Z of the Nigeria Education Sector Renewal Initiative (NESRI), bringing together the reforms, programmes, achievements and opportunities across our education system.

I invite every Nigerian to visit https://t.co/CsTj6TKlsr and explore the A–Z of NESRI.

If you are a parent, find out what opportunities are available for your children. If you are a student, explore the programmes you can benefit from. If you are a teacher, see what support is available.

And if something is not working as it should in your community, I want to hear about it. Your feedback will help us identify problems and address them.

Our journey from reform to opportunities and shared prosperity must begin with education.

The circumstances of a child’s birth should never determine the limits of their ambition. Our responsibility is to give every Nigerian child a fair chance to fulfil their potential.

We have more work to do, and I am determined to see it through.

Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR
President

2118004988433641835.text:
One of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was "composition"—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win. And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic. There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up. 

So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we're going to shock the world? "No," he told me. "We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us."

Well, that looks prophetic now. Our voters did show up. In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024. Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.  

There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true. 

But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone. 

Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points. I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this. In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats. He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were:

1) End the war
2) Focus on cost of living/inflation
3) Put America First
4) Change our relationship to Israel

Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results. While many spent Monday attacking Rachel Campos Duffy for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, it turns out her political advice was sound. (She’s also a great person.)

In the next few months, there's going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you. 

The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. 

If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.

But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.

I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, “I told you so”: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.

Last night was special.

Election days just never get old for us at Polymarket. Watching regular people experience the beauty of market based forecasts as the results come in. How practically useful it is. How simple it is to interpret. When it clicks, it clicks.

I know the industry has gained a mixed rap for a variety of reasons, many of which are criticisms with real merit. But I think I speak for both myself and my peers when I say we got into this because we really love the idea of markets being able to place a price on the future (e.g. Democrats had a 92% chance to take the House on Polymarket), and how that can help people better understand what's likely to happen and make decisions accordingly.

Our mission is to make sure we deliver on the promise of prediction markets, which was on full display last night. In the midst of so much noise around what we do, the American people get to see what Polymarket is really all about. Feels like one step closer to the dream. Onwards.
